options: As long and comprehensive as possible
A realistic 2-3 tools you'll actually use
Fixed and never allowed to change
The same for every person regardless of their triggers
questions.explanation: A short, realistic toolkit matched to your actual triggers is more useful than an exhaustive list.

questions.question: According to this module, a stress management plan should be:
options: Set once and never revisited
Reviewed and adjusted periodically
Abandoned if one week goes poorly
Followed perfectly every single day
questions.explanation: Regular review keeps the plan realistic and current as circumstances change.

questions.question: In short bursts, the body's stress response can:
options: Only ever be harmful
Sharpen focus and mobilize energy usefully
Immediately cause illness
Have no effect at all
questions.explanation: Short-term stress can sharpen focus and energy; sustained, unrecovered stress is what causes harm.

questions.question: Sleep and stress are related in that:
options: They are unrelated
They feed into each other in both directions
Only sleep affects stress, not the reverse
Improving one never helps the other
questions.explanation: Stress disrupts sleep, and poor sleep worsens stress reactivity, forming a two-way cycle.

questions.question: A breathing technique recommended in this course involves:
options: Breathing out for longer than you breathe in
Holding your breath as long as possible
Breathing as fast as possible
Breathing in for longer than you breathe out
questions.explanation: Extending the exhale relative to the inhale helps signal safety to the body and reduce tension.

questions.question: This course frames urgent and important tasks as:
options: Always the same thing
Different dimensions that should be sorted separately
Irrelevant to managing stress
Something only managers need to think about
questions.explanation: Distinguishing urgency from importance helps direct limited energy to what matters most.

questions.question: A respectful way to decline a request you don't have capacity for is to:
options: Avoid responding at all
Give a brief, honest response about your capacity
Always say yes regardless
Provide a lengthy justification every time
questions.explanation: A brief, honest decline respects both your limits and the other person.

questions.question: This course frames movement and rest as useful for resilience because:
options: They guarantee stress will never happen again
Consistent, enjoyable habits build capacity over time
Only intense exercise counts
Rest is unproductive and should be minimized
questions.explanation: Consistent, sustainable habits build long-term resilience more than intensity or willpower alone.

questions.question: A personal stress plan works best when it is:
options: Set once and never revisited
Reviewed and adjusted as triggers and circumstances change
As long and complex as possible
Identical to everyone else's plan
questions.explanation: Regular review keeps a personal stress plan realistic and matched to current circumstances.

title: Psychological First Aid
description: Develop foundational skills for providing safe, humane and practical support to people experiencing distress or crisis.
shortDescription: Develop foundational skills for providing safe, humane and practical support to people experiencing distress or crisis.
outcomes: Explain the purpose and limits of psychological first aid.
Apply Look, Listen and Link principles.
Communicate calmly and respectfully with distressed people.
Identify safeguarding and referral needs.
Protect personal boundaries and helper wellbeing.
prerequisites: This course does not qualify learners to diagnose or provide clinical treatment.

modules.title: PFA Foundations
modules.description: Purpose, principles, scope and limitations.

lessons.title: What Psychological First Aid Is (and Isn't)
lessons.content:
What Psychological First Aid Is (and Isn't)

Psychological First Aid (PFA) is a humane, practical way of supporting people right after a distressing event — it is not therapy, counselling, or a clinical intervention.

What PFA Actually Involves

PFA focuses on safety, calm, connection to practical help, and respecting the person's own coping — not on analyzing what happened or diagnosing anyone.

What PFA Is Not

It is not pressuring someone to describe the traumatic event in detail, not psychotherapy, and not something that requires a clinical license to provide responsibly.

Why This Distinction Matters

Being clear about the limits of PFA protects both the person receiving support and the helper — it keeps expectations realistic and points people toward professional help when that's what's actually needed.

Reflection

  1. Why might it be harmful to push someone to describe a traumatic event in detail?
  2. What is one situation where PFA would be appropriate, and one where it wouldn't be enough?
lessons.activity: Write two short scenarios: one where PFA is an appropriate response, and one where the situation clearly requires professional or emergency intervention instead.

materials.title: PFA Scope Worksheet
materials.instructions: Write two short scenarios: one where PFA is an appropriate response, and one where the situation clearly requires professional or emergency intervention instead.

lessons.title: The Look, Listen, Link Framework
lessons.content:
The Look, Listen, Link Framework

PFA is commonly organized around three simple actions: Look, Listen, and Link — a structure the rest of this course builds on in detail.

Look

Before engaging, check for immediate safety risks, urgent medical needs, and who may need help first.

Listen

Approach calmly, introduce yourself, ask permission to help, and listen without pressuring someone to share more than they want to.

Link

Connect the person with practical needs, trusted people, and appropriate services — PFA is often more about connection than conversation.

Reflection

  1. Which of the three steps (Look, Listen, Link) feels least intuitive to you right now?
  2. Why does the order of these steps matter?
lessons.activity: Write one sentence describing what you would actually do at each of the three steps (Look, Listen, Link) if you encountered someone in acute distress today.

materials.title: Look Listen Link Overview Worksheet
materials.instructions: Write one sentence describing what you would actually do at each of the three steps (Look, Listen, Link) if you encountered someone in acute distress today.

lessons.title: Boundaries of the Helper Role
lessons.content:
Boundaries of the Helper Role

Providing PFA does not make someone a therapist, and understanding this boundary is part of doing it responsibly.

Confidentiality, With Limits

What someone shares should generally stay private, except where there's a safeguarding concern or risk to safety that requires escalation.

Know When to Refer

PFA is a first response, not a full solution — recognizing when someone needs professional support and helping them access it is part of the role, not a failure of it.

You Don't Need to Have All the Answers

Being present, calm, and connecting someone to the right resource is enough — PFA doesn't require solving the underlying problem yourself.

Reflection

  1. What would tell you a situation is beyond what PFA alone can offer?
  2. Why is confidentiality important, and when should it be broken?
lessons.activity: List two situations where a PFA helper should refer someone to professional support rather than continuing to provide support alone.

materials.title: Helper Boundaries Worksheet
materials.instructions: List two situations where a PFA helper should refer someone to professional support rather than continuing to provide support alone.

questions.question: Psychological First Aid is best described as:
options: A form of psychotherapy
A humane, practical way of supporting someone after a distressing event
A clinical diagnosis process
Something only licensed therapists can provide
questions.explanation: PFA is a practical, humane support response, not therapy or diagnosis.

questions.question: The three actions in the Look, Listen, Link framework are best summarized as:
options: Diagnose, treat, discharge
Check safety, listen without pressuring, connect to help
Interrogate, record, report
Ignore, wait, escalate
questions.explanation: Look checks safety, Listen means approaching calmly without pressure, and Link connects people to practical help.

questions.question: A PFA helper's confidentiality should be broken when:
options: Never, under any circumstance
There is a safeguarding concern or risk to safety
The helper simply feels like sharing
Only if asked by a stranger
questions.explanation: Confidentiality generally holds except where safeguarding or safety risks require escalation.

modules.title: Look
modules.description: Safety, urgent needs, distress signs and safeguarding concerns.

lessons.title: Scanning for Immediate Safety
lessons.content:
Scanning for Immediate Safety

Before engaging with anyone in distress, the first step is a quick scan of the environment for immediate danger — to both the person and yourself.

What to Scan For

Ongoing hazards, unstable structures, traffic, crowds, or anything that could cause further harm should be checked before approaching.

Your Own Safety Matters Too

You cannot help others effectively if you become a casualty yourself — assessing your own safety is not selfish, it's necessary.

Acting on What You Find

If there's immediate danger, moving someone to safety (if possible) or calling for appropriate emergency help comes before any other PFA step.

Reflection

  1. What kinds of hazards might be easy to overlook in a distressing situation?
  2. Why does checking your own safety come before helping others?
lessons.activity: List three types of immediate safety hazards you would scan for before approaching someone in distress in a public setting.

materials.title: Safety Scanning Worksheet
materials.instructions: List three types of immediate safety hazards you would scan for before approaching someone in distress in a public setting.

lessons.title: Recognizing Urgent Needs and Distress Signs
lessons.content:
Recognizing Urgent Needs and Distress Signs

Once immediate safety is addressed, the next part of 'Look' is noticing who needs help most urgently and what kind of help that is.

Physical and Medical Needs

Visible injury, extreme confusion, or signs of physical shock require medical attention before anything else.

Signs of Acute Distress

Shaking, disorientation, being unable to respond to questions, or extreme withdrawal can indicate someone needs a calmer, more gradual approach.

Prioritizing When Several People Need Help

When multiple people are affected, urgent physical needs and immediate danger generally take priority over emotional support, which can follow once safety is established.

Reflection

  1. What distress signs would tell you someone needs a slower, gentler approach?
  2. How would you decide who to help first if several people needed support?
lessons.activity: Describe how you would prioritize helping two people in distress at once: one with a visible injury and one who is shaking and disoriented but physically unharmed.

materials.title: Prioritizing Needs Worksheet
materials.instructions: Describe how you would prioritize helping two people in distress at once: one with a visible injury and one who is shaking and disoriented but physically unharmed.

lessons.title: Spotting Safeguarding Concerns
lessons.content:
Spotting Safeguarding Concerns

Part of 'Look' includes staying alert to signs that someone, especially a child or vulnerable adult, may be at risk beyond the immediate event.

What Might Raise Concern

Signs of ongoing abuse, neglect, or a vulnerable person being separated from a trusted caregiver are safeguarding concerns that go beyond typical PFA support.

You Don't Investigate — You Report

It is not the helper's role to investigate or confront a suspected safeguarding issue directly; the responsible action is reporting it to the appropriate authority or service.

When in Doubt, Escalate

If something feels concerning but unclear, it's safer to raise it with someone qualified to assess it than to dismiss it.

Reflection

  1. Why is reporting, rather than investigating, the appropriate response to a safeguarding concern?
  2. Who would you report a safeguarding concern to in your own community or organization?
lessons.activity: Write down who you would report a safeguarding concern to in your school, workplace, or community, and what information you would include.

materials.title: Safeguarding Reporting Worksheet
materials.instructions: Write down who you would report a safeguarding concern to in your school, workplace, or community, and what information you would include.

questions.question: Before approaching someone in distress, a PFA helper should first:
options: Start asking detailed questions immediately
Scan the environment for immediate safety risks, including their own
Ignore any surrounding hazards
Wait for the person to approach them instead
questions.explanation: Checking for immediate safety, including the helper's own, comes before engaging.

questions.question: When multiple people need help, this module recommends prioritizing:
options: Whoever asks first, regardless of need
Urgent physical needs and immediate danger first
Emotional support before anything else
The most talkative person
questions.explanation: Urgent physical safety needs generally take priority, with emotional support following.

questions.question: If a PFA helper notices a possible safeguarding concern, the appropriate action is to:
options: Investigate and confront the situation themselves
Report it to the appropriate authority or service
Ignore it unless certain
Discuss it publicly to raise awareness
questions.explanation: Helpers report safeguarding concerns to qualified authorities rather than investigating themselves.

modules.title: Listen
modules.description: Approach, consent, active listening and emotional validation.

lessons.title: Approaching Someone Respectfully
lessons.content:
Approaching Someone Respectfully

How you approach someone in distress shapes whether they feel safe enough to accept help at all.

Introduce Yourself Calmly

A calm tone, a simple introduction, and non-threatening body language help someone feel less overwhelmed by another person approaching them.

Ask Before You Assume

Asking 'Is it okay if I sit with you?' or 'Can I help?' respects the person's autonomy, rather than assuming they want company or conversation.

It's Okay If They Say No

Some people won't want help in that moment, and that's a valid response — staying nearby and available, without pushing, still matters.

Reflection

  1. Why might asking permission matter more than jumping straight into helping?
  2. How would you respond if someone declined your offer to help?
lessons.activity: Write out exactly what you would say to introduce yourself and ask permission to help someone who appears distressed but is a stranger to you.

materials.title: Approach and Consent Script Worksheet
materials.instructions: Write out exactly what you would say to introduce yourself and ask permission to help someone who appears distressed but is a stranger to you.

lessons.title: Active Listening Without Pressure
lessons.content:
Active Listening Without Pressure

Once someone accepts support, the goal is to listen in a way that helps them feel heard, without pressuring them to share more than they're ready to.

What Active Listening Looks Like

Giving full attention, not interrupting, and reflecting back what you hear ('it sounds like that was really frightening') shows genuine listening.

Never Push for Details

Asking someone to describe a traumatic event in detail is not necessary for PFA and can retraumatize them — let them share only what they choose to.

Silence Is Okay

Comfortable silence gives someone space to gather their thoughts; it doesn't need to be filled immediately.

Reflection

  1. Why can asking for detailed accounts of a traumatic event be harmful?
  2. What would you do if someone went quiet while talking to you?
lessons.activity: Practice active listening this week in an everyday conversation, focusing on reflecting back what you hear rather than jumping to advice, and note what you noticed.

materials.title: Active Listening Practice Sheet
materials.instructions: Practice active listening this week in an everyday conversation, focusing on reflecting back what you hear rather than jumping to advice, and note what you noticed.

lessons.title: Validating Without Minimizing
lessons.content:
Validating Without Minimizing

Validation means acknowledging someone's feelings as real and understandable, without dismissing or exaggerating them.

What Validation Sounds Like

'That makes sense given what happened' or 'It's understandable to feel that way' acknowledges someone's experience without judging it.

Avoid Common Minimizing Phrases

Phrases like 'it could be worse' or 'at least you're okay' can unintentionally dismiss what someone is feeling, even when meant kindly.

Validation Isn't Agreement With Every Interpretation

You can validate someone's feelings without necessarily agreeing with every conclusion they've drawn — feelings and facts can be handled separately.

Reflection

  1. What is a validating phrase you could use that doesn't minimize someone's experience?
  2. Why might 'it could be worse' feel dismissive, even when well-intentioned?
lessons.activity: Write three validating phrases you could use with someone in distress, and three common minimizing phrases to avoid.

materials.title: Validation Language Worksheet
materials.instructions: Write three validating phrases you could use with someone in distress, and three common minimizing phrases to avoid.

questions.question: Before offering help, this module recommends:
options: Assuming the person wants help and proceeding
Asking permission first, respecting their autonomy
Waiting silently without introducing yourself
Insisting they accept help
questions.explanation: Asking permission respects the person's autonomy rather than assuming what they want.

questions.question: This module says asking someone to describe a traumatic event in detail:
options: Is a required part of PFA
Is unnecessary for PFA and can retraumatize the person
Should always be done immediately
Has no effect on the person
questions.explanation: PFA does not require detailed accounts, and pushing for them can retraumatize someone.

questions.question: Validation, as described in this module, means:
options: Agreeing with every conclusion the person draws
Acknowledging someone's feelings as real and understandable
Telling them it could be worse
Dismissing their experience to keep them calm
questions.explanation: Validation acknowledges feelings as real without necessarily agreeing with every interpretation.

modules.title: Link
modules.description: Practical help, social supports, referrals and services.

lessons.title: Practical Help First
lessons.content:
Practical Help First

After looking and listening, connecting someone to what they actually need practically is often more valuable than continued conversation.

What 'Practical' Can Mean

Accurate information, water, a place to sit, help contacting family, or transport can matter more in the moment than discussing feelings.

Ask What They Need

Rather than assuming, asking 'what would be most helpful right now?' lets the person direct what kind of help matters to them.

Small Help Still Counts

You don't need to solve everything — helping with one practical task can meaningfully reduce someone's distress.

Reflection

  1. What practical needs are easy to overlook when focused on emotional support?
  2. Why might asking 'what would help right now?' work better than assuming?
lessons.activity: List five types of practical help a PFA helper might offer someone right after a distressing event.

materials.title: Practical Help Worksheet
materials.instructions: List five types of practical help a PFA helper might offer someone right after a distressing event.

lessons.title: Reconnecting With Social Support
lessons.content:
Reconnecting With Social Support

Helping someone reconnect with people they trust is one of the most valuable things a PFA helper can do.

Why Social Connection Matters

Family, friends, or community members can offer ongoing support that a one-time helper cannot — reconnecting someone with their existing network extends the help beyond the immediate moment.

Helping Practically

This might mean helping someone contact a family member, find a trusted neighbor, or reach a community leader they know.

Respecting Their Choices

Not everyone wants the same people contacted — ask who they'd like reached, rather than assuming.

Reflection

  1. Who are the kinds of people you'd help someone reconnect with after a distressing event?
  2. Why is it important to ask who they want contacted, rather than assuming?
lessons.activity: Describe how you would help someone reconnect with a trusted person after a distressing event, including how you'd find out who they want contacted.

materials.title: Social Reconnection Worksheet
materials.instructions: Describe how you would help someone reconnect with a trusted person after a distressing event, including how you'd find out who they want contacted.

lessons.title: Making Effective Referrals
lessons.content:
Making Effective Referrals

Knowing when and how to connect someone with professional services is a core part of the 'Link' step.

Know What's Available

Being familiar with local services — medical, mental health, safeguarding, emergency — before you need them makes referrals faster and more useful in the moment.

How to Refer Well

Explaining clearly what a service does, and offering to help someone contact it (rather than just naming it) increases the chance they actually follow through.

Follow Up Where Possible

Checking in afterward, if appropriate, shows continued care and can catch if a referral didn't work out as hoped.

Reflection

  1. What services in your own community would you want to know about in advance?
  2. Why does offering to help someone contact a service work better than just naming it?
lessons.activity: Research and list three real support services in your community (or accessible remotely) that you could refer someone to, and what each one provides.

materials.title: Referral Directory Worksheet
materials.instructions: Research and list three real support services in your community (or accessible remotely) that you could refer someone to, and what each one provides.

questions.question: This module suggests finding out what someone needs practically by:
options: Assuming what they need without asking
Asking what would be most helpful right now
Ignoring practical needs entirely
Only offering emotional support
questions.explanation: Asking what would help lets the person direct the kind of support that matters most to them.

questions.question: When helping someone reconnect with their social support, this module recommends:
options: Contacting whoever you think is best without asking
Asking who they'd like reached, rather than assuming
Avoiding contacting anyone
Only contacting professional services
questions.explanation: Respecting the person's choice about who to contact is part of respectful support.

questions.question: An effective referral, according to this module, involves:
options: Just naming a service and moving on
Explaining what the service does and offering to help make contact
Avoiding mentioning specific services
Referring to services you know nothing about
questions.explanation: Clear explanation and offering to help with contact increases the chance a referral is followed through.

modules.title: Special Considerations
modules.description: Children, grief, trauma, displacement and vulnerable groups.

lessons.title: Supporting Children in Distress
lessons.content:
Supporting Children in Distress

Children often need a different approach to PFA than adults, shaped by their developmental stage and dependence on trusted caregivers.

Reunite With Caregivers Quickly

For most children, being reunited with a trusted caregiver is the single most stabilizing thing that can happen — this should be a priority.

Simple, Honest Language

Using calm, simple, age-appropriate language, and being honest without overwhelming detail, helps children feel safer than vague reassurance or avoidance.

Let Caregivers Lead When Possible

Where a trusted caregiver is present, supporting them to support the child is usually more effective than a stranger intervening directly.

Reflection

  1. Why might reuniting a child with a caregiver matter more than direct emotional support from a stranger?
  2. What would age-appropriate honesty sound like with a young child after a frightening event?
lessons.activity: Write an example of simple, honest, age-appropriate language you could use to reassure a child after a frightening event, without minimizing or overwhelming them.

materials.title: Supporting Children Worksheet
materials.instructions: Write an example of simple, honest, age-appropriate language you could use to reassure a child after a frightening event, without minimizing or overwhelming them.

lessons.title: Grief and Loss
lessons.content:
Grief and Loss

Grief is a natural, individual response to loss, and PFA around grief focuses on presence and support rather than trying to fix or rush the process.

Grief Doesn't Follow a Script

People grieve differently — there is no single 'correct' timeline or set of stages everyone must pass through.

Avoid Common Unhelpful Phrases

Phrases like 'everything happens for a reason' or 'they're in a better place' can feel dismissive, even when meant kindly — simple presence is often more helpful.

Practical Support Still Matters

Helping with practical tasks during acute grief (food, logistics, information) can be as valuable as emotional presence.

Reflection

  1. Why might well-meaning phrases about grief sometimes feel unhelpful?
  2. What practical support could you offer someone experiencing acute grief?
lessons.activity: List two things you would avoid saying to someone grieving, and two things (words or actions) you would offer instead.

materials.title: Grief Support Worksheet
materials.instructions: List two things you would avoid saying to someone grieving, and two things (words or actions) you would offer instead.

lessons.title: Displacement and Vulnerable Groups
lessons.content:
Displacement and Vulnerable Groups

People who have been displaced, or who belong to groups facing additional barriers, may need extra consideration when providing PFA.

Added Layers of Stress

Displacement often brings loss of home, community, documents, and routine on top of the original distressing event — compounding what someone is coping with.

Cultural and Language Sensitivity

Being aware of language barriers, cultural norms around help-seeking, and avoiding assumptions helps support feel genuinely respectful rather than imposed.

Extra Vulnerability Requires Extra Care

Older adults, people with disabilities, and unaccompanied minors may face additional barriers to safety or services, and may need more deliberate follow-through on referrals.

Reflection

  1. What extra barriers might a displaced person face beyond the immediate distressing event?
  2. How could language or cultural differences affect how you offer support?
lessons.activity: Describe one adjustment you would make to your approach when supporting someone from a different cultural or language background than your own.

materials.title: Cultural Sensitivity Worksheet
materials.instructions: Describe one adjustment you would make to your approach when supporting someone from a different cultural or language background than your own.

questions.question: For most children in distress, this module identifies the most stabilizing priority as:
options: Detailed explanation of what happened
Being reunited with a trusted caregiver
Being left alone to process
Immediate professional therapy
questions.explanation: Reuniting a child with a trusted caregiver is usually the most stabilizing action available.

questions.question: This module describes grief as:
options: Following the same fixed stages for everyone
A natural, individual process without one correct timeline
Something that should be rushed
Best addressed only with cheerful reassurance
questions.explanation: Grief is individual, and there is no single required timeline or sequence.

questions.question: When supporting displaced or vulnerable groups, this module emphasizes:
options: Applying the same approach regardless of background
Cultural and language sensitivity, avoiding assumptions
Ignoring additional barriers they may face
Assuming their needs are identical to others
questions.explanation: Displaced and vulnerable groups often face added barriers that call for cultural sensitivity and extra care.

modules.title: Helper Safety and Practice
modules.description: Boundaries, self-care, documentation and scenario practice.

lessons.title: Protecting Your Own Boundaries
lessons.content:
Protecting Your Own Boundaries

Helpers who don't protect their own boundaries risk burning out or being unable to help effectively when it matters most.

You Are Not Obligated to Do Everything

Helping does not mean saying yes to every request or being available indefinitely — recognizing your own limits is part of responsible helping.

Emotional Boundaries

You can care about someone's situation without taking on their distress as your own — maintaining some emotional distance helps you stay useful rather than overwhelmed.

Know When to Step Back

If a situation exceeds your training, capacity, or safety, stepping back and referring on is the responsible choice, not a failure.

Reflection

  1. What is a sign that you're taking on more than you can sustainably handle as a helper?
  2. What would help you step back from a situation without feeling like you've failed?
lessons.activity: Write down two personal boundaries you would set for yourself if you were regularly providing PFA support to others.

materials.title: Helper Boundaries Worksheet
materials.instructions: Write down two personal boundaries you would set for yourself if you were regularly providing PFA support to others.

lessons.title: Helper Self-Care
lessons.content:
Helper Self-Care

Providing support to people in distress can be emotionally demanding, and looking after your own wellbeing is part of doing the role responsibly, not an afterthought.

Watch for Your Own Warning Signs

Fatigue, irritability, trouble sleeping, or feeling emotionally numb can indicate you need rest or support yourself.

Debrief When Possible

Talking through a difficult experience with a trusted colleague, supervisor, or your own support system helps process what you've witnessed.

Rest Is Part of the Role

Taking breaks and stepping back after intense periods of helping is not optional self-indulgence — it sustains your ability to keep helping others well.

Reflection

  1. What would be an early warning sign that you need support after helping someone in distress?
  2. Who could you debrief with after a difficult helping experience?
lessons.activity: Identify one person or resource you could debrief with after a difficult helping experience, and one self-care action you would commit to afterward.

materials.title: Helper Self-Care Worksheet
materials.instructions: Identify one person or resource you could debrief with after a difficult helping experience, and one self-care action you would commit to afterward.

lessons.title: Putting It Into Practice
lessons.content:
Putting It Into Practice

This final lesson brings together Look, Listen, and Link into a single practiced sequence, along with simple documentation habits.

Running Through the Sequence

Look for safety and urgent needs, Listen with permission and without pressure, and Link to practical help and services — practicing this sequence mentally builds readiness.

Simple Documentation

Where appropriate (such as in an organizational setting), noting basic facts — what happened, what was done, any referrals made — supports continuity of care and accountability.

Confidence Comes With Practice

PFA skills, like any practical skill, become more natural with repetition and reflection — it's normal to feel uncertain the first few times.

Reflection

  1. Walk through the Look, Listen, Link sequence for a scenario you might realistically encounter.
  2. What basic information would be useful to document after providing PFA in an organizational setting?
lessons.activity: Write a full walkthrough of how you would apply Look, Listen, and Link to one realistic scenario, including what you would document afterward.

materials.title: PFA Scenario Practice Worksheet
materials.instructions: Write a full walkthrough of how you would apply Look, Listen, and Link to one realistic scenario, including what you would document afterward.

questions.question: According to this module, stepping back from a situation that exceeds your capacity is:
options: A failure on the helper's part
A responsible choice, not a failure
Never appropriate
Only allowed for professionals
questions.explanation: Recognizing limits and referring on is part of responsible helping, not a failure.

questions.question: This module frames rest and debriefing after helping as:
options: Optional self-indulgence
Part of sustaining your ability to keep helping well
Unnecessary for volunteers
Only needed after extreme events
questions.explanation: Rest and debriefing sustain a helper's capacity and are part of doing the role responsibly.

questions.question: Simple documentation after providing PFA is useful because it:
options: Is required to diagnose the person
Supports continuity of care and accountability
Replaces the need for referrals
Should include a full personal history
questions.explanation: Basic documentation of what happened and what was done supports continuity and accountability, not diagnosis.

questions.question: Psychological First Aid is best described as:
options: A form of psychotherapy requiring a clinical license
A humane, practical way of supporting someone after a distressing event
A method for diagnosing trauma
Something reserved only for emergency professionals
questions.explanation: PFA is a practical, humane support response, not therapy, diagnosis, or a licensed-only activity.

questions.question: Before engaging with someone in distress, a helper should first:
options: Begin asking detailed questions immediately
Scan the environment for immediate safety risks, including their own
Assume they want to talk in detail
Wait for someone else to act
questions.explanation: Checking immediate safety, including the helper's own, comes first in the Look step.

questions.question: Asking someone to describe a traumatic event in detail during PFA is:
options: A required step
Unnecessary and can retraumatize the person
The main goal of PFA
Something to insist on
questions.explanation: PFA does not require detailed accounts, and pushing for them can cause additional harm.

questions.question: The 'Link' step of PFA primarily involves:
options: Diagnosing the underlying cause of distress
Connecting the person with practical help, trusted people, and services
Keeping the person isolated until professionals arrive
Providing medication
questions.explanation: Link focuses on connecting people with practical assistance and appropriate support.

questions.question: For most children in acute distress, the most stabilizing priority is:
options: A detailed explanation of events
Being reunited with a trusted caregiver
Being left alone
Immediate clinical intervention
questions.explanation: Reuniting a child with a trusted caregiver is usually the most stabilizing available action.

questions.question: If a PFA helper notices a safeguarding concern, the appropriate response is to:
options: Investigate it personally
Report it to the appropriate authority or service
Ignore it unless certain
Confront the suspected individual directly
questions.explanation: Helpers report safeguarding concerns rather than investigating or confronting them directly.

questions.question: This course frames helper self-care and boundaries as:
options: Optional and unrelated to good helping
Part of sustaining the ability to help others responsibly
A sign of weakness
Something to address only after burnout occurs
questions.explanation: Protecting boundaries and practicing self-care sustains a helper's capacity to keep helping well.

title: Leadership Foundations
description: Build the core skills required to lead effectively, communicate clearly, make decisions and positively influence others.
shortDescription: Build the core skills required to lead effectively, communicate clearly, make decisions and positively influence others.
outcomes: Describe key leadership behaviors and values.
Communicate with clarity and empathy.
Make responsible decisions and solve problems.
Build trust and accountability.
Create a personal leadership development plan.
prerequisites: No formal leadership experience required.

modules.title: Foundations of Leadership
modules.description: Detailed study and practical application of foundations of leadership.

lessons.title: Leadership Beyond Job Titles
lessons.content:
Leadership Beyond Job Titles

Leadership is a set of behaviors, not a job title — people without formal authority influence outcomes constantly through judgment, communication, and reliability.

What Actually Drives Influence

Credibility built over time, clear communication, and consistently following through on commitments earn influence that a title alone cannot.

Leading From Where You Are

A team member can lead a project's quality standard, a student can lead a group's focus, a volunteer can lead by example — none of this requires a formal position.

Authority Still Matters, But Isn't Everything

Formal authority can make some things easier (like allocating resources), but it doesn't automatically produce trust or genuine influence.

Reflection

  1. Describe a time you saw someone lead effectively without having formal authority.
  2. What is one behavior you could adopt this week to lead from where you currently are?
lessons.activity: Write about a specific situation where you could exercise leadership without needing a formal title, and what behavior would demonstrate it.

materials.title: Leadership Beyond Job Titles Worksheet
materials.instructions: Write about a specific situation where you could exercise leadership without needing a formal title, and what behavior would demonstrate it.

lessons.title: Values, Ethics and Responsibility
lessons.content:
Values, Ethics and Responsibility

Leaders make decisions that affect other people, which is why values and ethical judgment matter as much as competence.

Values in Action, Not Just Words

Stated values only matter if they show up in actual decisions, especially under pressure or when there's a cost to holding them.

Results Don't Excuse the Method

Achieving a good outcome through dishonest or unfair means undermines trust, even if it isn't immediately visible.

Owning Mistakes

Taking responsibility for a bad decision, and correcting the harm where possible, builds more credibility than pretending it didn't happen.

Reflection

  1. Describe a values-based decision that was difficult because of what it cost you.
  2. How do you typically respond when you realize you've made a mistake that affected others?
lessons.activity: Describe a real or hypothetical situation where the ethical choice and the easy choice were different, and explain what you would do.

materials.title: Values and Ethics Worksheet
materials.instructions: Describe a real or hypothetical situation where the ethical choice and the easy choice were different, and explain what you would do.

lessons.title: Self-Awareness and Leadership Style
lessons.content:
Self-Awareness and Leadership Style

Understanding your own strengths, blind spots, and default reactions is foundational to leading others well.

Strengths Overused Become Weaknesses

A decisive leader can become impulsive; a collaborative leader can become indecisive — the same trait helps or hurts depending on how much of it shows up.

Feedback Reveals What Self-Reflection Misses

Other people often notice patterns in your behavior that you can't see yourself, which is why seeking honest feedback matters.

Adapting Your Style to the Situation

Different situations call for different amounts of direction and support — a rigid, one-size-fits-all style limits effectiveness.

Reflection

  1. What is one strength of yours that could become a weakness if overused?
  2. Who could give you honest feedback about your blind spots, and when will you ask them?
lessons.activity: Ask someone who knows your work well for one piece of honest feedback about a blind spot, and write down what you learned.

materials.title: Self-Awareness Feedback Worksheet
materials.instructions: Ask someone who knows your work well for one piece of honest feedback about a blind spot, and write down what you learned.

questions.question: This module describes leadership as primarily:
options: A formal job title
A set of behaviors anyone can practice regardless of position
Something only managers can do
Unrelated to trust or credibility
questions.explanation: Leadership is framed as behavior and influence, available to anyone regardless of formal title.

questions.question: According to this module, achieving a good result through dishonest means:
options: Is always acceptable if the outcome is good
Still undermines trust, even if not immediately visible
Has no effect on leadership credibility
Is the fastest path to becoming a leader
questions.explanation: Results don't excuse unethical methods, since trust erodes even when the harm isn't immediately obvious.

questions.question: This module says a strength like decisiveness can become a weakness when:
options: It is never used
It is overused without adapting to the situation
Feedback is sought too often
It is paired with self-awareness
questions.explanation: Overused strengths can tip into weaknesses; adapting style to the situation matters.

modules.title: Vision, Goals and Decision-Making
modules.description: Detailed study and practical application of vision, goals and decision-making.

lessons.title: Turning Vision Into Direction
lessons.content:
Turning Vision Into Direction

A vision describes a meaningful future; leadership's job is turning that into priorities people can actually act on today.

Make the Purpose Understandable

People commit more to work when they understand why it matters, not just what they've been asked to do.

Translate Aspiration Into Observable Outcomes

A vague vision stays abstract until it's broken into specific, visible outcomes people can work toward and recognize when achieved.

Say No to What Doesn't Fit

Removing or declining work that conflicts with agreed priorities is often what makes a vision achievable, rather than adding more initiatives on top of it.

Reflection

  1. Think of a goal or project you're part of. What is its underlying purpose, in one sentence?
  2. What is one task currently competing for attention that doesn't fit that purpose?
lessons.activity: Pick a current goal or project and write one sentence explaining its underlying purpose, then identify one task that conflicts with it.

materials.title: Vision to Direction Worksheet
materials.instructions: Pick a current goal or project and write one sentence explaining its underlying purpose, then identify one task that conflicts with it.

lessons.title: Setting Goals and Accountability
lessons.content:
Setting Goals and Accountability

Goals become achievable when they have a clear outcome, a clear owner, a way to measure progress, and a review point.

Define Success Before Starting

Agreeing what 'done well' looks like before work begins prevents disagreement and rework later.

One Clear Owner Per Outcome

When responsibility is shared vaguely across a group, it often ends up owned by no one — assigning one accountable person per outcome avoids this.

Accountability Isn't Punishment

Accountability means clarity about commitments and honest follow-through, not blame when something goes wrong — that distinction changes how people respond to it.

Reflection

  1. Think of a goal you're responsible for. How would you know, concretely, that it succeeded?
  2. Is there a task in your life right now with unclear ownership? What would fix that?
lessons.activity: Write one current goal with a clear success measure, a named owner, and a review date.

materials.title: Goals and Accountability Worksheet
materials.instructions: Write one current goal with a clear success measure, a named owner, and a review date.

lessons.title: Making Better Decisions
lessons.content:
Making Better Decisions

Good decisions combine relevant evidence, awareness of risk, and timely judgment — knowing when to gather more information and when delay itself becomes the bigger risk.

Separate Facts From Assumptions

Confusing what you actually know with what you're assuming is one of the most common causes of poor decisions.

Seek Out Disagreement Before Committing

Actively asking for a dissenting view before finalizing a decision surfaces blind spots that agreement alone won't reveal.

Review Outcomes, Not Just Effort

Reviewing what actually happened after a decision — not just how hard everyone worked — is what improves judgment over time.

Reflection

  1. Recall a recent decision. What was fact, and what was assumption?
  2. Who could you ask for a dissenting view on a decision you're currently making?
lessons.activity: Describe a decision you're currently facing, listing what you know as fact versus what you're assuming, and who could offer a dissenting view.

materials.title: Better Decisions Worksheet
materials.instructions: Describe a decision you're currently facing, listing what you know as fact versus what you're assuming, and who could offer a dissenting view.

questions.question: This lesson says a vision becomes actionable primarily when:
options: It stays abstract and inspirational
It is translated into specific, observable outcomes
More initiatives are added on top of it
It is never questioned or revised
questions.explanation: Translating aspiration into observable outcomes is what makes a vision actionable.

questions.question: According to this lesson, when responsibility for an outcome is shared vaguely across a group:
options: It works better than clear ownership
It often ends up owned by no one
Accountability becomes automatic
Nothing changes
questions.explanation: Vague shared responsibility tends to result in no one actually owning the outcome.

questions.question: This lesson recommends improving decision quality by:
options: Avoiding any dissenting opinions
Actively seeking a dissenting view before finalizing a decision
Committing as fast as possible regardless of evidence
Never reviewing outcomes afterward
questions.explanation: Seeking dissenting views before committing helps surface blind spots.

modules.title: Communication and Influence
modules.description: Detailed study and practical application of communication and influence.

lessons.title: Listening as a Leadership Skill
lessons.content:
Listening as a Leadership Skill

Leaders who genuinely listen access information that hierarchy otherwise hides — people are far less likely to raise problems with someone who doesn't seem to be listening.

Don't Prepare Your Rebuttal While Listening

Formulating your response while someone is still talking means you're not actually hearing them — genuine listening means holding off until they've finished.

Ask Before You Assume

Open questions surface information that assumptions would have missed entirely.

Make It Safe to Raise Bad News

If people are punished or dismissed for raising problems, they stop raising them — and leaders end up finding out too late.

Reflection

  1. When did you last catch yourself preparing a response instead of fully listening?
  2. How would people around you know it's safe to bring you bad news?
lessons.activity: In your next real conversation, practice not formulating your response until the other person has completely finished speaking, and note what you noticed.

materials.title: Active Listening Worksheet
materials.instructions: In your next real conversation, practice not formulating your response until the other person has completely finished speaking, and note what you noticed.

lessons.title: Giving Feedback That Changes Behaviour
lessons.content:
Giving Feedback That Changes Behaviour

Useful feedback is specific, timely, and focused on observable behavior and its impact — not on labeling someone's character.

Describe Behavior, Not Character

'You missed the deadline and didn't flag it' is actionable; 'you're unreliable' is a label that invites defensiveness instead of change.

Explain the Impact

Connecting the behavior to its actual consequence helps someone understand why it matters, not just that it was noticed.

Agree a Concrete Next Step

Feedback without a clear next action tends to be forgotten — ending with a specific, agreed step makes change more likely.

Reflection

  1. Think of feedback you've given recently. Was it about behavior or about character?
  2. What's one piece of feedback you need to give that you've been avoiding?
lessons.activity: Write out a piece of feedback you need to give, following the pattern: describe the behavior, explain the impact, agree a next step.

materials.title: Feedback Worksheet
materials.instructions: Write out a piece of feedback you need to give, following the pattern: describe the behavior, explain the impact, agree a next step.

lessons.title: Influencing Without Formal Authority
lessons.content:
Influencing Without Formal Authority

Influence grows when someone understands what others actually care about, builds credibility over time, and frames requests around mutual benefit.

Understand What People Actually Care About

Tailoring a message to what matters to the other person is far more persuasive than repeating your own priorities louder.

Evidence and Relationships, Not Pressure

Sustainable influence comes from credibility and genuine relationships — manipulation or pressure might work once, but it erodes trust for next time.

Make Commitments Visible and Reciprocal

Following through on your own commitments, visibly, makes it easier to ask others to follow through on theirs.

Reflection

  1. Think of someone you need to influence without formal authority. What do they actually care about?
  2. What is one commitment you could make visible to build credibility with them?
lessons.activity: Identify someone you need to influence without formal authority, and write one message framed around what they actually care about rather than what you want.

materials.title: Influence Without Authority Worksheet
materials.instructions: Identify someone you need to influence without formal authority, and write one message framed around what they actually care about rather than what you want.

questions.question: This lesson says preparing your rebuttal while someone is still speaking:
options: Is a sign of good listening
Means you're not actually hearing them
Has no effect on listening quality
Should be done to save time
questions.explanation: Formulating a response while someone talks interferes with genuinely hearing them.

questions.question: This lesson recommends giving feedback by:
options: Labeling the person's character
Describing observable behavior and its impact
Avoiding any mention of impact
Never agreeing on a next step
questions.explanation: Effective feedback focuses on specific behavior and impact rather than character labels.

questions.question: This lesson describes sustainable influence as coming from:
options: Pressure and manipulation
Credibility and genuine relationships
Repeating your own priorities louder
Formal authority alone
questions.explanation: Credibility and relationships sustain influence, while pressure erodes trust over time.

modules.title: Teams, Delegation and Conflict
modules.description: Detailed study and practical application of teams, delegation and conflict.

lessons.title: Building Trust and Psychological Safety
lessons.content:
Building Trust and Psychological Safety

High-performing teams need enough safety to ask questions, admit mistakes, and challenge ideas — safety doesn't remove accountability, it just makes honest information available sooner.

Respond Well When Problems Surface

How a leader reacts the first time someone raises a mistake sets the tone for whether people will raise the next one.

Separate Learning From Blame

Treating an honest mistake as a learning opportunity, rather than automatically assigning blame, keeps information flowing rather than getting hidden.

Address Disrespect, Don't Normalize It

Letting disrespectful behavior slide, even once, signals that it's tolerated — which quietly erodes the safety the team needs.

Reflection

  1. Think of a time someone raised a mistake with you. How did you respond, and what did that teach them?
  2. Is there a moment of disrespect you let slide that you should address?
lessons.activity: Describe a recent situation where someone raised a problem or mistake with you, and evaluate whether your response made it more or less likely they'd do so again.

materials.title: Psychological Safety Worksheet
materials.instructions: Describe a recent situation where someone raised a problem or mistake with you, and evaluate whether your response made it more or less likely they'd do so again.

lessons.title: Delegating for Ownership
lessons.content:
Delegating for Ownership

Delegation means transferring real responsibility for an outcome, with appropriate authority and support — not simply dumping tasks or retaining every decision yourself.

Explain the Outcome, Not Just the Task

Telling someone what to do without explaining why it matters produces compliance, not ownership.

Clarify What They Can Decide

Being explicit about which decisions are theirs to make, and which need to come back to you, prevents both micromanagement and confusion.

Review at Checkpoints, Not Constantly

Checking in at agreed points respects someone's ownership; hovering over every step undermines it.

Reflection

  1. Think of something you've delegated. Did you explain the outcome and why it mattered, or just the task?
  2. Are you currently micromanaging something you should be reviewing at checkpoints instead?
lessons.activity: Identify one task you're currently delegating or should delegate, and write out the outcome, the decision rights you'll grant, and your planned checkpoint.

materials.title: Delegation Worksheet
materials.instructions: Identify one task you're currently delegating or should delegate, and write out the outcome, the decision rights you'll grant, and your planned checkpoint.

lessons.title: Managing Conflict Constructively
lessons.content:
Managing Conflict Constructively

Conflict often exposes real differences in goals, information, or values — handled well, it can lead to a better outcome rather than lasting damage.

Address It Before Resentment Hardens

Small unresolved tensions tend to compound over time; addressing an issue early is usually easier than after resentment sets in.

Separate Positions From Underlying Interests

What someone is asking for (their position) and why they want it (their interest) are often different — understanding the interest opens up more possible solutions.

Silence Isn't Agreement

Assuming quiet means consensus can mean real disagreement goes unaddressed until it resurfaces later, often worse.

Reflection

  1. Think of an unresolved tension you've been avoiding. What's stopping you from addressing it?
  2. In a recent disagreement, what was the other person's underlying interest beneath their stated position?
lessons.activity: Describe a current or recent conflict, identifying the other person's stated position versus their likely underlying interest.

materials.title: Constructive Conflict Worksheet
materials.instructions: Describe a current or recent conflict, identifying the other person's stated position versus their likely underlying interest.

questions.question: This lesson says the way a leader responds the first time someone raises a mistake:
options: Has no effect on future behavior
Sets the tone for whether people will raise the next one
Should always involve blame
Is irrelevant to psychological safety
questions.explanation: The first response to a raised mistake shapes whether people feel safe raising future ones.

questions.question: According to this lesson, effective delegation requires:
options: Retaining every decision yourself
Explaining the outcome and clarifying decision rights
Assigning tasks without any context
Reviewing every step continuously
questions.explanation: Real delegation includes explaining why the outcome matters and clarifying what the person can decide.

questions.question: This lesson warns against assuming that silence means:
options: Disagreement
Agreement
Confusion
Nothing in particular
questions.explanation: Silence is not reliable evidence of agreement, and unaddressed disagreement can resurface later.

modules.title: Execution and Change
modules.description: Detailed study and practical application of execution and change.

lessons.title: Leading Through Change
lessons.content:
Leading Through Change

Change creates uncertainty about roles, competence, and workload — leaders who address that uncertainty directly get better adoption than those who just announce the change.

Communicate What's Known and What Isn't

Pretending to have all the answers when you don't erodes trust; being honest about what's still undecided builds more credibility.

Different People Are Affected Differently

The same change can be exciting for one person and threatening for another, depending on their role — a single message rarely lands the same way for everyone.

Train Before You Expect New Performance

Announcing a change and expecting immediate competence sets people up to fail; support and training need to come before the expectation.

Reflection

  1. Think of a change you've been part of. Was there enough honesty about what wasn't yet known?
  2. Who would be affected differently by a change you're currently leading or experiencing?
lessons.activity: Think of a change you're leading or experiencing, and write what is genuinely known versus still unknown, and who is affected differently by it.

materials.title: Leading Through Change Worksheet
materials.instructions: Think of a change you're leading or experiencing, and write what is genuinely known versus still unknown, and who is affected differently by it.

lessons.title: Managing Risk and Priorities
lessons.content:
Managing Risk and Priorities

Leadership requires deciding what deserves attention right now — and not every urgent-feeling request is actually strategically important.

Urgent Isn't Always Important

Some requests demand immediate attention but don't move you toward what actually matters — distinguishing the two protects your priorities.

Assign Clear Risk Owners

A risk without a named owner tends to get monitored by no one until it becomes a crisis.

Reprioritize When Evidence Changes

Sticking to a plan after the underlying facts have changed isn't discipline — it's a failure to adapt.

Reflection

  1. What is a currently 'urgent' request in your life that isn't actually strategically important?
  2. Is there a risk you're aware of that doesn't currently have a clear owner?
lessons.activity: List your top 3 current priorities, and identify one 'urgent' task competing for your attention that isn't actually one of them.

materials.title: Risk and Priorities Worksheet
materials.instructions: List your top 3 current priorities, and identify one 'urgent' task competing for your attention that isn't actually one of them.

lessons.title: Reviewing Performance and Learning
lessons.content:
Reviewing Performance and Learning

Execution improves through regular, honest review of what worked, what didn't, and why — not just moving straight to the next task.

Measure What Actually Matters

Metrics should connect to the real intended outcome, not just be easy to track — and should never be manipulated to look better than reality.

Capture Lessons While They're Fresh

Waiting too long to reflect on what happened means details and honest impressions fade — review works best close to the event.

Turn Lessons Into Actual Change

A lesson that doesn't change future behavior or process wasn't really learned — it was just noticed.

Reflection

  1. Think of a recent project or task. What metric would honestly reflect whether it succeeded?
  2. What is one lesson from a recent experience that you haven't yet turned into a changed behavior?
lessons.activity: Pick a recent project or task and write what worked, what didn't, why, and one specific change you'll make next time as a result.

materials.title: Performance Review Worksheet
materials.instructions: Pick a recent project or task and write what worked, what didn't, why, and one specific change you'll make next time as a result.

questions.question: This lesson says leaders build more credibility during change by:
options: Pretending to have all the answers
Being honest about what's known and what isn't
Avoiding communication until everything is decided
Announcing the change once and moving on
questions.explanation: Honesty about uncertainty builds more trust than pretending to have complete answers.

questions.question: According to this lesson, a risk without a named owner tends to:
options: Resolve itself automatically
Get monitored by no one until it becomes a crisis
Become less important over time
Require less attention than owned risks
questions.explanation: Unowned risks tend to go unmonitored until they escalate.

questions.question: This lesson says a lesson that doesn't change future behavior or process:
options: Was successfully learned
Was only noticed, not really learned
Should be repeated more often
Is more valuable than an applied lesson
questions.explanation: A lesson only counts as learned once it changes future behavior or process.

modules.title: Personal Leadership Practice
modules.description: Detailed study and practical application of personal leadership practice.

lessons.title: Resilience and Emotional Regulation
lessons.content:
Resilience and Emotional Regulation

Leaders shape the emotional climate around them, whether they intend to or not — how you handle pressure influences how everyone else responds to it too.

Name the Trigger Before Acting

Identifying what specifically triggered a strong reaction, before responding, creates a moment to choose rather than just react.

Pause Before High-Stakes Conversations

A brief pause to prepare, rather than responding immediately in a charged moment, usually produces a better outcome than an instant reaction.

Recovery Supports Judgment

Rest and recovery aren't indulgent extras — depleted energy makes emotional regulation and clear judgment measurably harder.

Reflection

  1. What typically triggers your strongest reactions as a leader or team member?
  2. What would help you pause before responding in a high-stakes moment?
lessons.activity: Identify your most common emotional trigger in a leadership or work context, and write one pause strategy you'll use next time it happens.

materials.title: Emotional Regulation Worksheet
materials.instructions: Identify your most common emotional trigger in a leadership or work context, and write one pause strategy you'll use next time it happens.

lessons.title: Leading Inclusively
lessons.content:
Leading Inclusively

Inclusive leadership means deliberately creating access to information, participation, and opportunity across differences — not assuming it happens automatically.

Invite Contribution in More Than One Way

Some people speak up easily in a group; others contribute better in writing or one-on-one — offering multiple formats surfaces more voices.

Check Outcomes, Not Just Intentions

Good intentions don't guarantee fair outcomes — actually checking who gets opportunities, and who doesn't, reveals what intentions alone can miss.

Challenge Disrespect Directly

Letting a disrespectful comment pass unaddressed signals, by silence, that it's acceptable.

Reflection

  1. Whose voice is typically missing or quieter in groups you're part of?
  2. What is one way you could check whether opportunities are actually being distributed fairly?
lessons.activity: Identify one group or team you're part of, and describe whose voice tends to be underrepresented and one specific way to invite it in.

materials.title: Inclusive Leadership Worksheet
materials.instructions: Identify one group or team you're part of, and describe whose voice tends to be underrepresented and one specific way to invite it in.

lessons.title: Creating a Leadership Development Plan
lessons.content:
Creating a Leadership Development Plan

Leadership improves through deliberate practice and honest feedback — not by waiting to feel ready.

Choose Behaviors, Not Vague Traits

'Be more confident' isn't practicable; 'speak up with one idea in every team meeting' is — specific behaviors can actually be practiced and measured.

Practice in Real Situations

Development happens fastest through real, low-stakes practice opportunities, not just reading or reflecting about leadership.

Collect Feedback From More Than One Source

A single perspective can be biased or incomplete — feedback from multiple people gives a more reliable picture of what's actually changing.

Reflection

  1. What is one specific, practicable behavior (not a vague trait) you want to develop?
  2. Who are two different people who could give you honest feedback on it?
lessons.activity: Write a simple development plan: one specific behavior to practice, one real situation to practice it in this week, and two people who will give you feedback.

materials.title: Leadership Development Plan Worksheet
materials.instructions: Write a simple development plan: one specific behavior to practice, one real situation to practice it in this week, and two people who will give you feedback.

questions.question: This lesson says naming a trigger before acting on it:
options: Wastes valuable time
Creates a moment to choose rather than just react
Makes the trigger more intense
Is unrelated to emotional regulation
questions.explanation: Naming a trigger before reacting creates space to choose a response deliberately.

questions.question: According to this lesson, good intentions around inclusion:
options: Automatically guarantee fair outcomes
Don't guarantee fair outcomes, so outcomes should be checked directly
Are irrelevant to leadership
Are more important than actual outcomes
questions.explanation: Checking actual outcomes reveals gaps that good intentions alone can miss.

questions.question: This lesson recommends a leadership development plan built around:
options: Vague traits like 'be more confident'
Specific, practicable behaviors with feedback from multiple people
A single feedback source
Waiting to feel ready before practicing
questions.explanation: Specific behaviors and multi-source feedback make development concrete and measurable.

questions.question: This course describes leadership as primarily:
options: A formal job title
A set of behaviors anyone can practice regardless of position
Something only managers can do
Unrelated to trust or credibility
questions.explanation: Leadership is framed as behavior and influence, available to anyone regardless of formal title.

questions.question: According to this course, achieving a good result through dishonest means:

title: Student Leadership
description: Develop confidence, communication, teamwork, responsibility and leadership skills for school and university environments.
shortDescription: Develop confidence, communication, teamwork, responsibility and leadership skills for school and university environments.
outcomes: Practice responsible student leadership.
Speak confidently and respectfully.

modules.title: Student Leadership Mindset
modules.description: Service, responsibility, integrity and positive influence.

lessons.title: Leadership Without a Title
lessons.content:
Leadership Without a Title

Student leadership doesn't require being class president or team captain — it's about the choice to take responsibility and act in ways that help others, regardless of your official role.

Service Over Status

Genuine student leaders focus on how they can help their class, club, or team function better, rather than on the recognition of holding a title.

Leading by Example

Showing up prepared, following through on commitments, and treating people respectfully influences others more than any speech, even without a formal position.

Anyone Can Start Today

Helping a struggling classmate, organizing a small group project well, or speaking up respectfully in class are all real acts of leadership available to any student right now.

Reflection

  1. Describe a time you (or someone you know) led without having an official title.
  2. What is one small way you could show leadership at school this week?
lessons.activity: Identify one situation at school or in an activity where you could demonstrate leadership this week, without needing an official title, and describe what you would do.

materials.title: Leadership Without a Title Worksheet
materials.instructions: Identify one situation at school or in an activity where you could demonstrate leadership this week, without needing an official title, and describe what you would do.

lessons.title: Integrity and Responsibility
lessons.content:
Integrity and Responsibility

Trust is the foundation of student leadership, and trust is built through consistent integrity, not just good intentions.

Doing What You Said You'd Do

Following through on commitments, even small ones like showing up on time for a group meeting, builds a reputation people can rely on.

Owning Mistakes

Admitting when you got something wrong, rather than blaming others or hiding it, actually builds more respect than pretending to be perfect.

Fairness Matters

Treating people consistently — not playing favorites among friends versus others in a group — is something peers notice quickly, for better or worse.

Reflection

  1. Think of someone you consider trustworthy. What specific behaviors make you trust them?
  2. Describe a time you made a mistake in a group setting. How did you handle it?
lessons.activity: Write about a time you had to admit a mistake in front of others, and what you would do the same or differently now.

materials.title: Integrity and Responsibility Worksheet
materials.instructions: Write about a time you had to admit a mistake in front of others, and what you would do the same or differently now.

lessons.title: Positive Influence Among Peers
lessons.content:
Positive Influence Among Peers

Peer influence can go either direction — toward better choices or worse ones. Student leaders are deliberate about which direction they push.

Influence Is Already Happening

Whether you intend to or not, your behavior affects how people around you act — being aware of this is the first step to using it well.

Standing Up Respectfully

Disagreeing with a group decision, or refusing to go along with something harmful, takes courage but is one of the clearest forms of positive leadership.

Encouraging Others

Noticing and encouraging someone else's effort or good idea, especially publicly, is a simple but powerful form of positive influence.

Reflection

  1. Describe a time you were influenced by a peer, positively or negatively.
  2. What is one way you could use your own influence more intentionally?
lessons.activity: Write about one specific way you could use positive peer influence this week, such as encouraging someone or respectfully pushing back on a bad group decision.

materials.title: Positive Peer Influence Worksheet
materials.instructions: Write about one specific way you could use positive peer influence this week, such as encouraging someone or respectfully pushing back on a bad group decision.

options: Holding an official title like class president
The choice to take responsibility and help others, regardless of role
Being the most popular student
Waiting to be given authority before acting
questions.explanation: Leadership is framed as a choice available to any student, not something requiring a title.
