lessons.title: Evaluating Sources and Downloading Safely
lessons.content:
Evaluating Sources and Downloading Safely

Not everything that appears in search results is accurate or safe — a little evaluation before trusting or downloading something goes a long way.

Check Who Actually Published the Information

A government, university, or established organization's website is generally more reliable than an anonymous blog or an unfamiliar site — check the "About" page or author if you're unsure.

Cross-Check Important Information

If a claim matters (health information, financial advice, a statistic you plan to use), checking it against at least one other credible source reduces the risk of relying on something wrong.

Only Download From Sources You Trust

Before downloading a file, consider whether the website is legitimate and whether the file type makes sense for what you're downloading — unexpected pop-ups urging an immediate download are a common warning sign.

Reflection

  1. Describe a time you weren't sure whether information online was accurate. How did you check it?
  2. What are two signs that a website or download link might not be trustworthy?

lessons.title: Structuring an Email People Will Actually Read
lessons.content:
Structuring an Email People Will Actually Read

A clear, well-structured email gets read and acted on faster than a long, disorganized one.

Write a Subject Line That Says What It's About

"Question" tells the reader nothing; "Question about Tuesday's meeting time" lets them know instantly what it's about and helps them find it again later.

Keep the Message Focused and Scannable

Opening with the purpose of the email, keeping paragraphs short, and using a clear closing (what you need, and by when) makes an email far easier to act on quickly.

Use To, Cc and Bcc Deliberately

"To" is for people who need to act; "Cc" is for people who just need to stay informed; "Bcc" hides recipients from each other, useful for large group emails where privacy matters.

Reflection

  1. Look at a recent email you sent. Did the subject line clearly describe its content?
  2. Describe a situation where using Cc or Bcc appropriately would matter.

lessons.title: Attachments and Links Without the Mistakes
lessons.content:
Attachments and Links Without the Mistakes

Two of the most common email frustrations — forgotten attachments and confusing links — are both easy to avoid with a habit change.

Attach the File Before You Write "Attached Is..."

Attaching the file first, before writing the body of the email, prevents the common mistake of sending "see attached" with nothing actually attached.

Check File Size and Format Before Sending

Very large files may fail to send or get rejected by the recipient's inbox — compressing files or using a shared cloud link instead avoids this problem.

Make Links Clear About Where They Lead

Pasting a long, unclear web address makes recipients hesitant to click — a short description of what the link leads to builds trust and gets it clicked.

Reflection

  1. Have you ever sent an email saying "see attached" without actually attaching anything? What helped you catch it, or what would help next time?
  2. Describe a link you received that felt untrustworthy. What made it feel that way?
lessons.activity: Practice attaching a real file to a draft email before writing the message, and write a link in an email draft with a clear description of where it leads.

lessons.title: Professional Email Etiquette
lessons.content:
Professional Email Etiquette

Email tone is easy to misjudge — a message that felt neutral while writing it can read as curt or cold to the person receiving it.

Match Your Tone to the Relationship

A message to a close colleague can be brief and casual; a message to someone you don't know well, or a person in authority, benefits from a greeting, a clear request, and a polite closing.

Reply Within a Reasonable Time

Even a short "got this, will respond properly by Thursday" is better than silence — it shows the message was received and sets a clear expectation.

Reread Before You Send

A quick reread catches typos, missing attachments, an unclear ask, or a tone that might land differently than intended — a small habit that prevents real problems.

Reflection

  1. Describe a time an email's tone was misread, by you or someone else. What might have caused it?
  2. What is your current habit around rereading emails before sending, and is it working?

lessons.title: Documents That Look Right and Stay Consistent
lessons.content:
Documents That Look Right and Stay Consistent

Word processors (Microsoft Word, Google Docs) do more than let you type — using their structure features makes documents easier to read and update.

Use Headings Instead of Just Bold Text

Applying a real heading style, rather than just making text bold and bigger, lets you generate a table of contents automatically and keeps formatting consistent throughout the document.

Formatting Consistency Signals Professionalism

Mixed fonts, inconsistent spacing, and random font sizes make a document look unpolished even if the content is strong — picking one style and sticking to it matters.

Track Changes and Comments Support Collaboration

When multiple people work on a document, Track Changes shows exactly what was edited, and Comments let people ask questions without changing the actual text.

Reflection

  1. Look at a document you created recently. Did you use heading styles, or just bold text?
  2. Describe a time inconsistent formatting made a document harder to read or use.

lessons.title: Spreadsheets: Rows, Columns and Simple Formulas
lessons.content:
Spreadsheets: Rows, Columns and Simple Formulas

A spreadsheet (Excel, Google Sheets) organizes information into a grid of rows and columns, and its real power comes from simple formulas that do calculations automatically.

Each Cell Has an Address

A cell like B3 refers to column B, row 3 — formulas reference these addresses so calculations update automatically when the underlying numbers change.

Basic Formulas Save Real Time

A formula like =SUM(A1:A10) adds a range of numbers instantly, and updates automatically if any of those numbers change — far faster and more accurate than adding manually.

Sort and Filter to Find What You Need

Sorting arranges rows by a chosen column (like alphabetically or by amount); filtering temporarily hides rows that don't match a condition, making a large spreadsheet easier to work with.

Reflection

  1. Describe a real task where a simple spreadsheet formula could save you time over doing it by hand.
  2. Have you used sorting or filtering in a spreadsheet before? What did it help you find?

lessons.title: Presentations and Cloud Storage That Work for You
lessons.content:
Presentations and Cloud Storage That Work for You

Presentation software (PowerPoint, Google Slides) and cloud storage (Google Drive, OneDrive) are two tools most people use often but rarely use well.

Fewer Words, Bigger Ideas

A slide packed with text is hard for an audience to read and listen at the same time — a short headline and one key visual or point per slide communicates more effectively.

Consistent Design Beats Flashy Design

Using one template, one font, and a consistent color scheme throughout looks more professional than mixing several different styles across slides.

Cloud Storage Enables Real-Time Collaboration

Files stored in the cloud can be edited by multiple people at once, accessed from any device, and are automatically backed up — a real advantage over emailing files back and forth.

Reflection

  1. Think of a presentation you've seen that was hard to follow. What made it hard?
  2. What is one file you currently only keep on one device that would benefit from being in cloud storage?

lessons.title: Building Passwords That Actually Protect You
lessons.content:
Building Passwords That Actually Protect You

A weak or reused password is one of the most common ways accounts get broken into — and it's also one of the easiest things to fix.

Length and Uniqueness Beat Complexity Tricks

A long password (12+ characters), ideally a random phrase, is harder to guess than a short one with substituted symbols — and using a different password for each important account limits the damage if one is exposed.

A Password Manager Solves the Memory Problem

Password managers generate and store strong, unique passwords for every account, so you only need to remember one master password — far more practical than trying to memorize dozens.

Two-Factor Authentication Adds a Real Second Layer

Two-factor authentication (a code sent to your phone, or an authenticator app) means a stolen password alone usually isn't enough to get into your account — enabling it on email and banking apps meaningfully reduces risk.

Reflection

  1. How many of your important accounts currently use the same or a similar password?
  2. Which accounts do you not yet have two-factor authentication enabled on?

lessons.title: Spotting Phishing Before It Works
lessons.content:
Spotting Phishing Before It Works

Phishing is a fake message designed to trick you into giving up a password, clicking a dangerous link, or sending money — and the messages are often convincingly disguised.

Urgency and Fear Are Common Red Flags

Messages demanding you act immediately ("your account will be suspended in 1 hour") are designed to make you act before thinking — genuine organizations rarely create that kind of pressure.

Check the Actual Sender, Not Just the Display Name

A message that looks like it's from a bank or company can have a sender address that doesn't actually match — checking the full email address, not just the display name, reveals many fakes.

When Unsure, Verify Independently

Instead of clicking a link in a suspicious message, going directly to the organization's known website or calling their official number confirms whether the message was real.

Reflection

  1. Have you ever received a message that felt like it was pressuring you to act quickly? What tipped you off, if anything?
  2. What is your plan the next time you receive a message asking for a password or payment?

lessons.title: Protecting Your Privacy and Using Devices Responsibly
lessons.content:
Protecting Your Privacy and Using Devices Responsibly

Small daily habits around updates, sharing, and screen time meaningfully affect how safe and healthy your digital life is.

Keep Software Updated

Updates frequently patch security vulnerabilities — delaying them longer than necessary leaves known weaknesses open on your device.

Think Before You Share Personal Information

Location, full birthdate, and other personal details shared publicly or with unfamiliar apps can be used in ways you didn't intend — checking privacy settings periodically helps limit this.

Responsible Use Includes Your Own Wellbeing

Digital safety isn't only about hackers — noticing when screen time is affecting your sleep, focus, or mood, and setting boundaries around it, is also part of using technology responsibly.

Reflection

  1. When did you last check the privacy settings on an app or account you use regularly?
  2. Is there a digital habit (notifications, screen time, oversharing) you'd like to change? What's one small step toward that?

lessons.title: Finding Your Way Around Word
lessons.content:
Finding Your Way Around Word

Microsoft Word's screen looks busy at first, but almost everything you'll ever need sits in one place: the Ribbon.

The Ribbon Groups Tools by Task

Tabs like Home, Insert, and Layout each hold a Ribbon full of related buttons — Home for text formatting, Insert for images and tables, Layout for margins and orientation. Knowing which tab holds what saves constant searching.

The Document Area Is Where You Actually Type

The large white space is your page. The blinking cursor (insertion point) shows exactly where the next character you type will appear — clicking anywhere in existing text moves it there.

Zoom and View Controls Change How You See, Not the Document

The zoom slider (bottom right) and View tab only change how large the page looks on your screen — they never affect the actual document or what prints.

Reflection

  1. Open Word and identify three different Ribbon tabs. What kind of tools does each one group together?
  2. What is the difference between the cursor position and your mouse pointer position?

lessons.title: Creating, Saving and Naming Documents
lessons.content:
Creating, Saving and Naming Documents

Losing unsaved work is one of the most common and most avoidable frustrations in computer use.

Save Early and Save Often

Pressing Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on Mac) the moment you start a document, and again every few minutes, means a crash or accidental close costs you almost nothing.

Choose a File Format That Matches the Purpose

The default .docx format keeps the document editable; saving as PDF instead locks the layout so it looks the same on any device — useful for a final version you don't want changed.

AutoSave and AutoRecover Are a Safety Net, Not a Plan

Word can automatically save versions in the background, but relying on this alone (instead of your own habit of saving) is risky if the feature is off or the file is stored somewhere it can't reach.

Reflection

  1. Have you ever lost work because you forgot to save? What would have prevented it?
  2. When would you save a document as a PDF instead of leaving it as .docx?

lessons.title: Basic Editing: Selecting, Moving and Undoing
lessons.content:
Basic Editing: Selecting, Moving and Undoing

A handful of editing habits make working in Word dramatically faster than clicking and retyping everything.

Select Before You Act

Almost every formatting or editing action applies to whatever text is currently selected (highlighted) — double-click selects a word, triple-click selects a paragraph, and Ctrl+A selects everything.

Cut, Copy and Paste Move Text Without Retyping

Ctrl+X (cut), Ctrl+C (copy), and Ctrl+V (paste) let you move or duplicate text instantly — far faster and more accurate than deleting and retyping.

Undo Is Your Safety Net for Mistakes

Ctrl+Z instantly reverses your last action, and can be pressed repeatedly to step back through several changes — there's rarely a reason to panic over a mistake.

Reflection

  1. Which of these keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X, Ctrl+V, Ctrl+Z) do you already use, and which are new to you?
  2. Describe a time retyping something instead of using cut/copy/paste cost you real time.

Lock the layout so it looks the same on any device
Make the file editable by anyone

modules.title: Text and Paragraph Formatting
modules.description: Fonts, spacing, alignment, bullets and numbering.

lessons.title: Choosing Fonts That Actually Work
lessons.content:
Choosing Fonts That Actually Work

Font choice affects how easily a document is read, and how professional it looks, more than most people realize.

Fewer Fonts Look More Professional

Mixing four or five different fonts in one document looks chaotic — sticking to one or two (a heading font and a body font) looks intentional and polished.

Readable Sizes Depend on Purpose

Body text is typically 11-12pt for a printed document; headings are larger to create visual hierarchy so a reader can scan the structure at a glance.

Bold, Italic and Underline Have Different Jobs

Bold draws attention to key terms, italic is used for emphasis or titles, and underline is largely reserved for links now — using all three at once on the same text usually looks cluttered, not important.

Reflection

  1. Look at a document you've written recently. How many different fonts did you use, and was that intentional?
  2. When would bold be more appropriate than italic, or vice versa?
lessons.activity: Take a paragraph of practice text and format it three different ways (heading font, body size, selective bold), then explain which version is most readable and why.

lessons.title: Spacing and Alignment That Signal Structure
lessons.content:
Spacing and Alignment That Signal Structure

Line spacing and alignment quietly communicate how a document should be read, even before anyone reads a single word.

Line Spacing Affects Readability

Single spacing looks dense and can tire a reader over a long document; 1.15-1.5 line spacing gives text room to breathe without wasting excessive space.

Alignment Should Match the Content Type

Left alignment is easiest to read for most body text; centered alignment suits short titles or headings, not paragraphs, which become harder to read when every line starts in a different place.

Consistent Paragraph Spacing Beats Manual Blank Lines

Setting "space after paragraph" in the formatting options creates consistent gaps automatically — pressing Enter twice between every paragraph is a common habit that creates uneven, hard-to-fix spacing.

Reflection

  1. Have you noticed a document that was hard to read because of poor spacing or alignment? What was off about it?
  2. Why might centered alignment be a poor choice for a long paragraph?
lessons.activity: Take a multi-paragraph practice document, apply 1.15 line spacing and consistent paragraph spacing (not manual blank lines), and left-align the body text.

materials.title: Spacing and Alignment Worksheet
materials.instructions: Take a multi-paragraph practice document, apply 1.15 line spacing and consistent paragraph spacing (not manual blank lines), and left-align the body text.

lessons.title: Bullets and Numbering for Clear Lists
lessons.content:
Bullets and Numbering for Clear Lists

Lists break up dense information, but only if you choose the right type and keep them consistent.

Use Numbers for Order, Bullets for No Order

Numbered lists imply sequence or ranking (steps, priorities); bullet points imply the items are related but not ordered — using the wrong one can quietly confuse a reader.

Let Word Handle the Numbering

Using the built-in numbered list tool automatically renumbers if you add or remove an item — typing numbers manually means fixing every single one by hand after any change.

Keep List Items Grammatically Consistent

If one bullet starts with a verb, the others should too — mixing sentence fragments with full sentences in the same list looks unpolished, even if each item makes sense alone.

Reflection

  1. Think of a list you've written. Should it have used numbers instead of bullets, or vice versa?
  2. Why does manually typing list numbers cause more work later?
lessons.activity: Create one numbered list (a sequence of steps) and one bulleted list (unordered related items) using Word's built-in list tools, then add and remove an item from the numbered list to confirm it renumbers automatically.

materials.title: Lists Worksheet
materials.instructions: Create one numbered list (a sequence of steps) and one bulleted list (unordered related items) using Word's built-in list tools, then add and remove an item from the numbered list to confirm it renumbers automatically.

options: As many as possible for variety
One or two, such as a heading font and a body font
A different font for every paragraph
Exactly five fonts
questions.explanation: Sticking to one or two fonts looks intentional and professional, while mixing many looks chaotic.

questions.question: According to this module, centered alignment is best suited for:
options: Long body paragraphs
Short titles or headings
Every part of a document
Numbered lists only
questions.explanation: Centered alignment suits short headings; long paragraphs become harder to read when centered.

questions.question: This module recommends using Word's built-in numbered list tool instead of typing numbers manually because:
options: It looks more colorful
It automatically renumbers when items are added or removed
It is required for all lists
It replaces the need for bullet points entirely

modules.title: Page Layout
modules.description: Margins, orientation, breaks, headers, footers and page numbers.

lessons.title: Margins, Orientation and Paper Size
lessons.content:
Margins, Orientation and Paper Size

These three settings, found under the Layout tab, determine the basic shape of every page in your document.

Margins Control the Usable Space

Margins are the blank border around each page — narrower margins fit more content per page, but very narrow margins can make a document look cramped or get cut off when printed.

Orientation Should Match the Content

Portrait (tall) suits most text documents; landscape (wide) suits wide tables, charts, or certificates — choosing the wrong one often forces awkward shrinking or wrapping.

Paper Size Affects How a Document Prints

Most documents default to a standard size like A4 or Letter — checking this before sending a document for printing avoids a layout that looks right on screen but prints incorrectly.

Reflection

  1. When would landscape orientation genuinely be more appropriate than portrait?
  2. Have you ever opened a document and the margins or orientation looked wrong for the content? What would have fixed it?
lessons.activity: Create a practice document with a wide table or chart, and set it to landscape orientation with appropriate margins to fit the content cleanly.

materials.title: Margins and Orientation Worksheet
materials.instructions: Create a practice document with a wide table or chart, and set it to landscape orientation with appropriate margins to fit the content cleanly.

lessons.title: Page Breaks and Section Breaks
lessons.content:
Page Breaks and Section Breaks

Pressing Enter repeatedly to push text onto the next page is one of the most common formatting mistakes, and it causes real problems later.

A Page Break Moves Content Cleanly

Inserting an actual page break (Insert > Page Break) forces the next content to start on a new page reliably — unlike blank lines, it won't shift out of place when you edit earlier text.

Section Breaks Allow Different Formatting Per Part

A section break lets one part of a document have different margins, orientation, or headers than another — useful when, for example, a landscape table needs to sit inside an otherwise portrait report.

Why Manual Blank Lines Cause Problems Later

Blank lines used to push content down will shift unpredictably any time earlier content is edited, added, or removed — a genuine page break stays exactly where you put it.

Reflection

  1. Have you used blank lines to force a new page before? What happened when you edited the content above it?
  2. Describe a document that might need a section break (different formatting in different parts).
lessons.activity: In a practice document, replace a stack of blank lines with an actual page break, then add earlier content and confirm the break stays in place correctly.

lessons.title: Headers, Footers and Page Numbers
lessons.content:
Headers, Footers and Page Numbers

Headers, footers, and page numbers help a reader navigate a longer document and make it look properly finished.

Headers and Footers Repeat Automatically

Text added to a header or footer (like a document title or your name) appears on every page automatically — you only need to set it once.

Page Numbers Should Match the Document's Needs

Word can insert page numbers that update automatically as content is added or removed — far more reliable than typing a number onto each page by hand.

Different First Page Is a Common, Useful Option

Many documents (like reports or certificates) suppress the header or page number on the title page only — a built-in option, not something you need to fake by deleting text manually.

Reflection

  1. What information would be useful in the header or footer of a document you create often?
  2. Why might a document's title page not show a page number, even though page 2 does?
lessons.activity: Add a header with a document title and an automatically updating page number to a multi-page practice document, and enable a different first page.

Nothing but a title page
questions.explanation: Landscape orientation suits wide content like tables and charts better than portrait.

options: Makes editing more difficult
Stays in place reliably even when earlier content changes
Only works in landscape orientation
Removes the need for section breaks

modules.title: Tables and Visuals
modules.description: Tables, images, shapes and captions.

lessons.title: Building a Table That Communicates Clearly
lessons.content:
Building a Table That Communicates Clearly

A table organizes information into rows and columns so a reader can compare values at a glance — but a poorly built one can be more confusing than plain text.

Insert a Table With the Right Size From the Start

Using Insert > Table and specifying rows and columns upfront avoids the messy workaround of using the Tab key and spaces to fake a grid, which never aligns properly.

Header Rows Should Be Visually Distinct

Bolding or shading the first row helps a reader immediately identify column labels, rather than having to guess what each column means.

Keep Tables Simple, Not Cluttered

A table with too many merged cells or inconsistent columns becomes hard to read — when a table gets that complex, it may work better as two simpler tables.

Reflection

  1. Describe a piece of information you've seen written as a paragraph that would have been clearer in a table.
  2. Why does using Tab and spaces to fake a table cause problems later?
lessons.activity: Create a real table (at least 3 columns, 4 rows) using Word's Insert Table tool, with a bolded header row, for information you actually need to organize.

materials.title: Building Tables Worksheet
materials.instructions: Create a real table (at least 3 columns, 4 rows) using Word's Insert Table tool, with a bolded header row, for information you actually need to organize.

lessons.title: Adding and Sizing Images Properly
lessons.content:
Adding and Sizing Images Properly

Images can make a document far more engaging, but poorly placed images are one of the most common causes of a document looking broken.

Text Wrapping Controls How Text Flows Around an Image

The default wrapping often locks an image in place awkwardly — changing the wrapping option (like "Square" or "Tight") lets text flow naturally around it instead of leaving strange gaps.

Resize Proportionally to Avoid Distortion

Dragging a corner handle (not a side or top/bottom handle) resizes an image while keeping its proportions — dragging the wrong handle stretches or squashes it.

Compress Images to Keep File Size Manageable

Large, uncompressed photos can make a document huge and slow to email — Word's built-in compress picture tool reduces file size with minimal visible quality loss.

Reflection

  1. Have you seen a document where an image looked stretched or oddly placed? What likely caused it?
  2. Why might a very large document file size become a real problem for sharing?
lessons.activity: Insert an image into a practice document, resize it proportionally using a corner handle, and adjust its text wrapping so surrounding text flows naturally.

materials.title: Working With Images Worksheet
materials.instructions: Insert an image into a practice document, resize it proportionally using a corner handle, and adjust its text wrapping so surrounding text flows naturally.

lessons.title: Captions and Labeling Visuals
lessons.content:
Captions and Labeling Visuals

An image or table without a caption forces a reader to guess what it's showing and why it's there.

Captions Give Context in One Line

A short caption under an image or table (like "Figure 1: Monthly attendance by school") tells a reader exactly what they're looking at without needing to reread the surrounding paragraph.

Word's Caption Tool Numbers Automatically

Using Insert > Caption instead of typing "Figure 1" manually means captions renumber automatically if you reorder or add images later.

Reference Figures by Number in Your Text

Writing "as shown in Figure 1" in the body text, rather than just "as shown below", keeps the reference accurate even if the image later moves to a different page.

Reflection

  1. Why is referencing "Figure 1" more reliable than saying "the image below"?
  2. Look at a document with images or tables you've made. Did it have clear captions?
lessons.activity: Add a properly numbered caption to an image or table in a practice document using Word's Caption tool, and reference it by number in a nearby sentence.

options: Using Tab and spaces to fake a grid
Using Insert Table with the rows and columns specified upfront
Typing each row as a separate paragraph
Avoiding tables entirely
questions.explanation: Using the actual Insert Table tool avoids the alignment problems caused by faking a grid with tabs and spaces.

modules.title: Styles and Review
modules.description: Styles, find/replace, comments and proofreading.

lessons.title: Using Styles Instead of Manual Formatting
lessons.content:
Using Styles Instead of Manual Formatting

Manually formatting every heading one at a time is slow, inconsistent, and makes a document much harder to update later.

Styles Apply Consistent Formatting Instantly

Selecting text and clicking a style like Heading 1 applies a whole set of formatting (font, size, color, spacing) at once — and updates everywhere that style is used if you change the style definition.

Styles Enable an Automatic Table of Contents

A table of contents built from real heading styles updates automatically as the document changes — one built by manually typing page numbers breaks the moment anything shifts.

Consistency Across a Document Signals Quality

A document where every heading looks slightly different (some bold, some a different size) looks unfinished, even if the content itself is strong.

Reflection

  1. Have you formatted headings manually before instead of using styles? What made updating them difficult?
  2. Why does a document built from real styles look more professional than one formatted by hand?
lessons.activity: Take a practice document with several headings, apply real Word heading styles to them, then insert an automatic table of contents.

materials.title: Using Styles Worksheet
materials.instructions: Take a practice document with several headings, apply real Word heading styles to them, then insert an automatic table of contents.

lessons.title: Find, Replace and Navigating Long Documents
lessons.content:
Find, Replace and Navigating Long Documents

Scrolling through a long document looking for one word, or fixing the same mistake repeated many times, wastes real time that a couple of tools eliminate.

Find Jumps You Straight to What You Need

Ctrl+F opens a search that highlights every match in the document and lets you jump between them — far faster than scrolling and scanning manually.

Replace Fixes Repeated Mistakes at Once

Ctrl+H can replace every instance of a misspelled name or outdated term throughout a document in seconds — reviewing each replacement before confirming avoids accidentally changing something you didn't intend.

The Navigation Pane Shows a Document's Structure

With heading styles applied, the Navigation pane lists every heading as a clickable outline — letting you jump to any section instantly in a long document.

Reflection

  1. Describe a time scrolling through a long document to find something wasted real time.
  2. Why is it worth reviewing each match before confirming a Replace All?
lessons.activity: In a long practice document, use Find to locate a specific word, then use Replace to correct a repeated term, reviewing each match before confirming.

materials.title: Find and Replace Worksheet
materials.instructions: In a long practice document, use Find to locate a specific word, then use Replace to correct a repeated term, reviewing each match before confirming.

lessons.title: Comments, Track Changes and Proofreading
lessons.content:
Comments, Track Changes and Proofreading

Before a document goes out, a review pass catches problems that are hard to spot while writing.

Comments Let You Ask Questions Without Changing the Text

Insert > Comment attaches a note to specific text without altering it — useful for flagging a question or suggestion for someone else to address.

Track Changes Shows Exactly What Was Edited

Turning on Track Changes records every edit as a visible change that can be accepted or rejected individually — essential when multiple people work on the same document.

Spelling and Grammar Check Catches What Tired Eyes Miss

The built-in checker catches many errors automatically, but it doesn't catch everything (like a correctly spelled wrong word) — reading the document aloud once catches mistakes a quick scan misses.

Reflection

  1. Why might a spelling checker miss a word that's spelled correctly but used incorrectly?
  2. Describe a situation where Track Changes would be more useful than just editing directly.

An automatic table of contents that updates as the document changes
Headings to look different from each other
Removing the need for headings entirely
questions.explanation: Real heading styles enable an automatically updating table of contents, unlike manually formatted headings.

options: Confirming Replace All without reviewing matches

questions.explanation: Reviewing matches before replacing avoids accidentally changing something unintended.

modules.title: Professional Document Project
modules.description: Create, review, export and present a finished document.

lessons.title: Planning the Document Before Opening Word
lessons.content:
Planning the Document Before Opening Word

The strongest documents are planned before the first word is typed, not figured out along the way.

Know Your Audience and Purpose First

Who will read this, and what do they need to walk away knowing or able to do? A CV, a report, and a flyer all demand different structure, tone, and length — deciding this first shapes every choice that follows.

Outline the Structure Before Writing

Sketching the headings and sections first (even as a rough list) keeps the writing focused and makes it far easier to reorganize than restructuring finished prose.

Decide the Final Format Early

Knowing whether the final document will be printed, emailed as PDF, or edited further by someone else affects decisions about page count, file format, and how much design polish is worth the time.

Reflection

  1. Think of a real document you need to create soon. Who is the audience, and what do they need from it?
  2. Why does planning structure before writing save time later?

lessons.title: Building the Full Document
lessons.content:
Building the Full Document

This is where everything from earlier modules comes together into one real, finished document.

Build Structure First, Polish Second

Get all the headings, sections, and rough content in place using real styles before spending time on fonts, images, or fine formatting — polishing content that later gets deleted wastes effort.

Use Real Content, Not Placeholder Text

Practicing with your actual CV, a real report, or genuine content makes the skills stick far better than generic filler text ever could.

Save Versions as You Go

Saving periodically with version-aware names (or using version history) means you can recover an earlier draft if a later change turns out to be a mistake.

Reflection

  1. What is the real document you're building in this project, and who is it actually for?
  2. What is one section you're unsure how to format, and which earlier lesson could help?

lessons.title: Reviewing, Exporting and Presenting the Final Document
lessons.content:
Reviewing, Exporting and Presenting the Final Document

A document isn't finished when the writing stops — the review and export step is what makes it genuinely ready to share.

Review Against a Real Checklist

Checking spelling and grammar, consistent formatting, working captions, and correct page numbers systematically catches more than a casual read-through.

Export to the Format Your Audience Needs

A CV going to an employer is usually safest as PDF (locks the layout); a report a colleague needs to edit should stay as .docx — choosing correctly avoids a frustrating back-and-forth.

Presenting Your Work Builds Real Confidence

Being able to explain the choices you made — why this structure, why this format — turns a finished document into demonstrated, explainable skill, not just a file.

Reflection

  1. Run through your document with a real checklist (spelling, formatting, captions, page numbers). What did you catch?
  2. Which export format does your finished document need, and why?

lessons.title: Understanding the Grid: Cells, Rows and Columns
lessons.content:
Understanding the Grid: Cells, Rows and Columns

Everything in Excel lives in a grid, and understanding how that grid is addressed is the foundation for everything else.

Every Cell Has a Unique Address

A cell address like B3 means column B, row 3 — this address is how formulas refer to data, so understanding it is essential before writing any formula.

A Workbook Can Hold Multiple Sheets

The tabs at the bottom of the screen are separate sheets within one workbook (file) — useful for keeping related data (like monthly budgets) organized without needing separate files.

A Range Is a Group of Cells

A range like A1:A10 refers to a block of cells at once — formulas and formatting can apply to a whole range instead of one cell at a time.

Reflection

  1. What is the cell address for the third column, fifth row?
  2. Why might someone use multiple sheets in one workbook instead of separate files?
lessons.activity: Open Excel, create a new workbook with two sheets, and enter sample data into a 3x3 range on the first sheet, noting the exact cell addresses you used.

lessons.title: Entering Data Correctly
lessons.content:
Entering Data Correctly

How data is entered determines whether Excel can actually calculate with it later — a small mistake here causes confusing errors down the line.

Numbers vs. Text: Excel Treats Them Differently

A number typed as plain digits can be calculated; the same digits entered with a stray space or symbol may be stored as text, which formulas can't add up — numbers align right by default, text aligns left, a quick visual check.

Use Fill Handle for Fast, Consistent Entry

Dragging the small square at a cell's corner (the fill handle) can continue a pattern — like dates or a numbered sequence — across many cells instantly instead of typing each one.

Avoid Retyping Data That Already Exists

Copy and paste, or referencing another cell directly, avoids the typos that come from retyping the same data more than once.

Reflection

  1. Have you ever entered a number that Excel treated as text? How did you notice?
  2. Describe a situation where the fill handle would save real time.

lessons.title: Basic Formatting for Readability
lessons.content:
Basic Formatting for Readability

A spreadsheet full of unformatted numbers is hard to read at a glance — a few formatting habits make data far easier to understand quickly.

Number Formats Should Match the Data

Currency, percentages, and dates each have a dedicated format that displays them correctly (like $1,200.00 or 15%) — typing symbols manually into a cell often breaks calculations.

Bold Headers and Borders Create Visual Structure

Bolding column headers and adding borders around a data range helps a reader immediately see where the table starts and what each column means.

Column Width Should Fit the Content

Double-clicking the border between two column letters auto-fits the width to the content — faster and more consistent than manually dragging each one.

Reflection

  1. Why might typing a $ symbol directly into a cell cause problems for calculations?
  2. Look at a spreadsheet you've made. Would bold headers or borders make it easier to read?

lessons.title: Writing Your First Formula
lessons.content:
Writing Your First Formula

Every formula in Excel starts the same way, and once that pattern clicks, calculations become simple.

Every Formula Starts With an Equals Sign

Typing =5+3 into a cell tells Excel to calculate, not just display, the text — without the equals sign, Excel treats it as plain text and won't calculate anything.

Formulas Can Reference Other Cells

Typing =A1+A2 adds whatever values are in those two cells — and updates automatically if either value changes, which is the real power of a spreadsheet over a calculator.

Operators Work the Way You'd Expect

Plus (+), minus (-), multiply (*), and divide (/) work in formulas the same way they do in math — and Excel follows standard order of operations (multiplication before addition, for example).

Reflection

  1. What is the difference between typing 8 and typing =5+3 into a cell?
  2. Why is referencing cells (like =A1+A2) more useful than typing =5+3 directly?
lessons.activity: In a practice sheet, enter numbers into three cells, then write a formula in a fourth cell that references and adds two of them together.

lessons.title: SUM, AVERAGE, MIN and MAX
lessons.content:
SUM, AVERAGE, MIN and MAX

These four functions cover a huge share of everyday spreadsheet work, and each answers a different, common question.

SUM Adds a Range Instantly

=SUM(A1:A10) adds every value in that range — far faster and more reliable than typing =A1+A2+A3... by hand, especially for long lists.

AVERAGE Finds the Typical Value

=AVERAGE(A1:A10) calculates the mean of a range automatically — useful for things like average scores or average monthly spending.

MIN and MAX Find the Extremes

=MIN(A1:A10) and =MAX(A1:A10) instantly find the smallest and largest values in a range — useful for spotting outliers without scanning manually.

Reflection

  1. Think of a real list of numbers you track (expenses, scores, attendance). Which of these four functions would be useful for it?
  2. Why is =SUM(A1:A10) more reliable than typing out every cell individually?
lessons.activity: Build a column of at least 8 numbers (real data if possible) and calculate its SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, and MAX using the actual functions, not manual calculation.

lessons.title: Copying Formulas Without Breaking Them
lessons.content:
Copying Formulas Without Breaking Them

Copying a formula down a column is one of Excel's most useful tricks — but it only works correctly if you understand how references behave.

Relative References Shift When Copied

A formula like =A1+B1 copied down one row automatically becomes =A2+B2 — this is usually exactly what you want when applying the same calculation to each row.

Absolute References Stay Fixed

Adding dollar signs, like $A$1, locks that reference so it doesn't shift when copied — essential when every row needs to reference one fixed value, like a tax rate in a single cell.

Always Check a Copied Formula's Result

After copying a formula down a column, spot-checking a few results against expectations catches reference mistakes before they spread through the whole sheet.

Reflection

  1. Describe a situation where you'd want a reference to stay fixed instead of shifting when copied.
  2. Why is it worth spot-checking a formula after copying it down many rows?

lessons.title: Turning a Range Into a Real Table
lessons.content:
Turning a Range Into a Real Table

Converting plain data into an actual Excel table unlocks features that a regular range doesn't have.

A Real Table Adds Structure Automatically

Insert > Table gives your data banded rows, a header row with filter buttons, and formulas that automatically extend to new rows added at the bottom.

Named Ranges Make Formulas Easier to Read

A table's columns get real names, so a formula can reference "Sales" instead of a vague range like C2:C50 — easier to read and less likely to reference the wrong column.

Tables Grow With Your Data

Adding a new row directly below a table automatically includes it in the table's formatting and formulas — a plain range requires manually extending formulas and formatting each time.

Reflection

  1. What is the difference between a plain range of data and a real Excel table?
  2. Why might named columns make formulas easier to understand later?

lessons.title: Sorting Data to Answer Real Questions
lessons.content:
Sorting Data to Answer Real Questions

Sorting rearranges rows to answer questions like "who scored highest?" or "what happened first?" instantly.

Sort by the Column That Matters

Selecting a column and choosing Sort A-Z (or largest to smallest for numbers) reorders every row based on that column, keeping each row's other data intact.

Select the Whole Table Before Sorting

Sorting only one column while leaving others unselected breaks the connection between related data in a row — always confirm the whole table is included before sorting.

Multi-Level Sort Answers More Complex Questions

Sorting by one column, then a second (like sorting by department, then by name within each department) organizes data in a way a single sort can't.

Reflection

  1. Think of a real list you have (grades, expenses, contacts). What question would sorting it answer?
  2. Why is it risky to sort just one column instead of the whole table?
lessons.activity: Take a table of at least 8 rows with two meaningful columns, and sort it two different ways to answer two different real questions about the data.

lessons.title: Filtering and Data Validation
lessons.content:
Filtering and Data Validation

Filtering shows only the rows you need without deleting anything; validation prevents bad data from being entered in the first place.

Filters Hide, They Don't Delete

Turning on a filter and selecting specific values temporarily hides non-matching rows — the data is still there, and clearing the filter brings it all back instantly.

Combine Filters to Narrow Down Precisely

Filtering by more than one column at once (like a date range and a category) narrows results to exactly what you need, faster than scanning manually.

Data Validation Prevents Errors Before They Happen

Setting a validation rule (like only allowing a date, or only values from a specific list) on a cell stops someone from entering something that doesn't belong there — catching mistakes at entry instead of after the fact.

Reflection

  1. Describe a situation where filtering a large list would save real time.
  2. Why is catching a data entry mistake at the point of entry better than fixing it later?

lessons.title: The IF Function: Decisions Inside a Cell
lessons.content:
The IF Function: Decisions Inside a Cell

IF lets a cell display different results depending on a condition — a small taste of real logic inside a spreadsheet.

IF Follows a Simple Three-Part Pattern

=IF(condition, value if true, value if false) — for example, =IF(B2>=50,"Pass","Fail") checks a score and displays Pass or Fail automatically for every row.

IF Saves You From Manually Checking Every Row

Copied down a column, one IF formula evaluates every row's condition instantly — instead of manually checking and labeling each one by hand.

Conditions Can Use Any Comparison

>, <, >=, <=, and = all work inside an IF condition, letting you check exactly the comparison you need, not just equality.

Reflection

  1. Think of a real yes/no decision in data you track. How could IF automate labeling it?
  2. Why is IF more efficient than manually checking each row of a long list?

lessons.title: COUNTIF and SUMIF: Conditional Counting and Adding
lessons.content:
COUNTIF and SUMIF: Conditional Counting and Adding

These two functions count or add only the values that match a condition — extremely common in real analysis.

COUNTIF Counts Matching Entries

=COUNTIF(A1:A20,"Present") counts how many cells in that range say "Present" — useful for quickly tallying attendance, categories, or responses.

SUMIF Adds Only What Matches

=SUMIF(A1:A20,"Books",B1:B20) adds the values in column B, but only for rows where column A says "Books" — a common need when summarizing spending or sales by category.

The Condition Range and Sum Range Must Line Up

SUMIF checks one range for the condition and sums a different (but matching-length) range — mismatched ranges silently produce a wrong number, not an error.

Reflection

  1. Think of a real list you track by category. What would COUNTIF or SUMIF calculate for you?
  2. Why is it important that the condition range and sum range in SUMIF are the same length?
lessons.activity: Build a list of categorized data (like expenses by type), then use COUNTIF to count entries in one category and SUMIF to total the amounts for that category.

lessons.title: Working With Text and Dates
lessons.content:
Working With Text and Dates

Not everything in a spreadsheet is a number — text and date functions handle the rest of what real data looks like.

Combine Text From Multiple Cells

=CONCATENATE(A2," ",B2) or the & operator (=A2&" "&B2) joins a first and last name from two cells into one — faster and less error-prone than retyping.

Excel Understands Real Dates, Not Just Text

A properly entered date can be added, subtracted, and sorted correctly (like calculating days between two dates) — a date typed in an unrecognized format is stored as plain text and can't be calculated with.

TODAY Updates Itself Automatically

=TODAY() always shows the current date whenever the sheet is opened — useful for calculating someone's age or days remaining without updating it manually.

Reflection

  1. Describe a situation where combining text from two columns (like first and last name) would be useful.
  2. Why might a date typed in an unusual format cause problems later in a spreadsheet?

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Chart Type
lessons.content:
Choosing the Right Chart Type

A chart's whole purpose is to make a pattern in the data obvious at a glance — but the wrong chart type can hide the pattern instead.

Bar and Column Charts Compare Categories

Best for comparing amounts across a few distinct categories, like sales by region or votes by candidate — easy to read at a glance.

Line Charts Show Change Over Time

Best for tracking a trend across days, months, or years — the connecting line makes direction and rate of change visible in a way a bar chart can't.

Pie Charts Show Parts of a Whole

Best for showing how something breaks down into proportions (like budget categories) — and only work well with a small number of slices; too many makes it unreadable.

Reflection

  1. Think of a real dataset you have. Would a bar, line, or pie chart best show its pattern?
  2. Why might a pie chart with 15 slices be a poor choice?

lessons.title: Conditional Formatting to Spot Patterns Instantly
lessons.content:
Conditional Formatting to Spot Patterns Instantly

Conditional formatting changes a cell's appearance automatically based on its value — turning a wall of numbers into something you can scan visually.

Highlight Values That Meet a Condition

Setting a rule like "highlight cells greater than 100 in red" instantly flags outliers or values worth attention, without manually scanning every row.

Color Scales Show Patterns Across a Whole Range

A color scale shades cells from low to high automatically — useful for spotting trends across a large table (like which months had the highest expenses) at a glance.

Rules Update Automatically as Data Changes

Unlike manually coloring cells by hand, conditional formatting re-evaluates automatically whenever the underlying data changes — no need to reapply formatting after an update.

Reflection

  1. Think of a real spreadsheet where highlighting values above or below a threshold would help.
  2. Why is conditional formatting more reliable than manually coloring cells by hand?

lessons.title: Building a Simple Summary With PivotTables
lessons.content:
Building a Simple Summary With PivotTables

A PivotTable turns a long list of raw data into a short, meaningful summary in just a few clicks.

PivotTables Summarize Without Formulas

Dragging a field into "Rows" and another into "Values" instantly totals or counts data by category — no SUMIF or COUNTIF formulas required for a quick summary.

Change the Summary Instantly by Rearranging Fields

Dragging a different field into Rows or Values re-summarizes the same data a completely different way, in seconds — far faster than rebuilding formulas manually.

PivotTables Update When You Refresh

If the source data changes, clicking Refresh updates the PivotTable's totals automatically — the summary doesn't need to be rebuilt from scratch.

Reflection

  1. Think of a long list of raw data you have. What summary would actually be useful from it?
  2. Why might a PivotTable be faster than manually writing several SUMIF formulas?

lessons.title: Planning Your Spreadsheet Before Building It
lessons.content:
Planning Your Spreadsheet Before Building It

The strongest spreadsheets are planned before the first cell is filled, not figured out row by row as you go.

Decide What Question the Spreadsheet Must Answer

A budget tracker, an attendance log, and a sales report all need different columns and structure — knowing the real question first ("where is my money going?") shapes every design choice.

Sketch the Columns Before Entering Data

Deciding column headers first (Date, Category, Amount, Notes) prevents the messy restructuring that comes from entering data first and figuring out structure later.

Plan for Data That Will Be Added Later

Building the sheet as a real table from the start, with room to grow, avoids having to rebuild formulas every time new rows are added.

Reflection

  1. Choose a real spreadsheet you want to build (budget, tracker, or report). What real question should it answer?
  2. What columns will it need to answer that question?

Building the Full Spreadsheet

This is where every skill from earlier modules comes together into one real, working spreadsheet.

Build the Table Structure First

Set up your real Excel table with proper headers and formatting before adding formulas — a clean structure makes every formula added afterward easier to get right.

Add Formulas That Actually Calculate What You Need

Use SUM, AVERAGE, IF, or SUMIF depending on what your specific project needs — a budget tracker might need SUMIF by category; an attendance log might need COUNTIF.

Use Real Data, Not Placeholder Numbers

Entering your actual expenses, real attendance, or genuine data makes the spreadsheet something you'll actually use afterward, not just a practice exercise.

Reflection

  1. What formulas does your specific project need, based on what you planned in the last lesson?
  2. What real data are you using to build this, and why does that matter?

lessons.title: Reviewing, Visualizing and Presenting Your Spreadsheet
lessons.content:
Reviewing, Visualizing and Presenting Your Spreadsheet

A spreadsheet isn't finished when the formulas work — reviewing and presenting it is what makes it genuinely usable and trustworthy.

Check Formulas Against Expected Results

Spot-checking a few calculated values by hand confirms formulas are working correctly — catching a reference error now is far easier than after the sheet has been shared and relied on.

Add a Chart or Summary for Quick Understanding

A simple chart or PivotTable summary lets someone understand the spreadsheet's key finding in seconds, without reading every row.

Explain Your Design Choices

Being able to explain why you chose specific columns, formulas, or chart types turns a finished spreadsheet into demonstrated, explainable skill.

Reflection

  1. Spot-check two calculated values in your spreadsheet by hand. Did they match?
  2. What is the one key insight your chart or summary reveals at a glance?

lessons.title: Getting Comfortable in the Canva Workspace
lessons.content:
Getting Comfortable in the Canva Workspace

Canva's layout looks simple, but knowing where things live saves real time once you're designing something with several elements.

The Canvas Is Your Design, the Panels Are Your Tools

The center area is what you're actually creating; the left panel holds templates, elements, and uploads; the top toolbar controls the specific element currently selected — what you click on changes what the toolbar shows.

Pages Let You Build Multi-Slide Designs

A presentation or multi-page document uses the Pages panel to add, duplicate, and reorder pages — duplicating a page keeps consistent styling far faster than rebuilding it.

Everything Autosaves as You Work

Canva saves your progress automatically, but naming your design clearly from the start still makes it much easier to find again later among many projects.

Reflection

  1. Open Canva and identify where templates, elements, and uploads each live in the interface.
  2. Why might duplicating a page be faster than building a new one from scratch?

lessons.title: Starting Smart: Templates and Elements
lessons.content:
Starting Smart: Templates and Elements

Starting from a blank page is much harder than adapting something already well-designed — Canva's templates and elements are built for exactly this.

Templates Are a Starting Point, Not a Final Product

A template gives you proven layout and spacing — but swapping in your own colors, text, and images is what makes it actually yours, not a copy everyone recognizes.

Elements Add Visual Interest Without Needing to Design From Scratch

Icons, shapes, lines, and illustrations from the Elements panel let you add visual structure without any drawing skill — searching by keyword finds relevant options quickly.

Group Related Elements Together

Selecting multiple elements and grouping them lets you move or resize them as one unit — much easier than repositioning each piece individually.

Reflection

  1. Why might starting from a template be faster than starting from a blank canvas, without making the result look generic?
  2. Describe a design you could improve by adding a simple icon or shape from Elements.
lessons.activity: Choose a Canva template, replace its text and colors with your own content, add at least two elements, and group them together.

lessons.title: Uploading Your Own Content and Exporting Correctly
lessons.content:
Uploading Your Own Content and Exporting Correctly

Getting your own images in, and getting the finished design out correctly, are the two steps that make Canva actually useful for real work.

Upload Your Own Images and Logos

The Uploads panel lets you bring in your own photos or logo, which then behave like any other element — draggable, resizable, and reusable across designs.

Choose the Right Export Format for the Purpose

PNG keeps a transparent background (good for logos); JPG is smaller for photos; PDF is best for print or documents meant to stay uneditable — choosing the wrong one causes real problems later.

Check Resolution Before Exporting for Print

A design meant for printing needs higher resolution than one only viewed on screen — Canva's export settings let you choose this before downloading.

Reflection

  1. Which export format would you use for a logo with a transparent background, and why?
  2. Why might a design that looks fine on screen print poorly if exported at the wrong resolution?
lessons.activity: Upload a real image or logo into a Canva design, then export the finished design twice: once as PNG and once as PDF, noting the difference.

modules.title: Design Principles
modules.description: Alignment, hierarchy, contrast, spacing and consistency.

lessons.title: Alignment and Hierarchy: Guiding the Eye
lessons.content:
Alignment and Hierarchy: Guiding the Eye

Before color or fonts, alignment and hierarchy determine whether a design feels organized or accidental.

Aligned Elements Create Invisible Order

Text and images lined up along shared edges (using Canva's alignment guides, which snap automatically) look intentional — elements scattered slightly off from each other create a subtle but real sense of sloppiness.

Hierarchy Tells the Viewer What to Read First

Making the most important text largest or boldest, with supporting details smaller, guides a viewer's eye in the order you intend — without hierarchy, everything competes for attention equally.

Whitespace Isn't Wasted Space

Empty space around elements gives a design room to breathe and makes the important parts stand out more — cramming every inch full usually makes a design harder to read, not more impressive.

Reflection

  1. Look at a design (poster, slide, app screen) you see often. Can you identify what's meant to be read first, second, third?
  2. Describe a design that felt cluttered. What role did whitespace (or lack of it) play?
lessons.activity: Take a design with at least three text elements and reorganize it using clear alignment and a visual hierarchy (one clearly biggest/boldest element, supporting details smaller).

materials.instructions: Take a design with at least three text elements and reorganize it using clear alignment and a visual hierarchy (one clearly biggest/boldest element, supporting details smaller).

lessons.title: Contrast That Actually Works
lessons.content:
Contrast That Actually Works

Contrast is what makes text readable and important elements noticeable — without it, even good content becomes hard to see.

Text Needs Real Contrast Against Its Background

Light gray text on a white background, or dark text on a busy photo, is genuinely hard to read — checking readability at actual size, not just zoomed in while editing, catches this.

Contrast Can Highlight, Not Just Improve Readability

A single bright button on an otherwise muted design draws the eye immediately — using contrast deliberately for the one thing you most want noticed.

Too Much Contrast Everywhere Cancels Itself Out

If every element competes for attention with bold contrast, nothing actually stands out — contrast works best when used selectively.

Reflection

  1. Have you seen a design where text was hard to read against its background? What would fix it?
  2. Describe a design element (a button, a headline) that used contrast well to grab your attention.
lessons.activity: Take a design with a readability problem (or create one deliberately), fix the text contrast against its background, and use contrast to highlight one key element.

materials.title: Contrast Worksheet
materials.instructions: Take a design with a readability problem (or create one deliberately), fix the text contrast against its background, and use contrast to highlight one key element.

lessons.title: Spacing and Consistency Across a Design
lessons.content:
Spacing and Consistency Across a Design

Consistent spacing and repeated style choices are what separate a design that feels professionally made from one that feels thrown together.

Consistent Spacing Between Elements Signals Care

Uneven gaps between elements (some tight, some wide) is subtle but noticeable — consistent spacing throughout makes a design feel more polished, even if the viewer can't say exactly why.

Repeat Style Choices Across a Multi-Page Design

Using the same font, color palette, and spacing rules across every page or slide of a design creates a cohesive set, rather than pages that feel unrelated.

Set Rules for Yourself Before You Start

Deciding your font pairing, color palette, and spacing pattern before designing multiple pieces keeps everything consistent without having to check back and forth constantly.

Reflection

  1. Look at a multi-page design (presentation, brochure). Did each page feel like part of the same set?
  2. What simple rules (font, color, spacing) could you set for yourself before starting your next design?
lessons.activity: Create a simple 2-3 page design using one consistent font pairing, color palette, and spacing pattern throughout, then note the specific rules you followed.

modules.title: Typography and Color
modules.description: Readable type, palettes and brand consistency.

lessons.title: Pairing Fonts That Work Together
lessons.content:
Pairing Fonts That Work Together

Font choice affects both how readable a design is and how it feels emotionally, before a viewer reads a single word.

One Heading Font, One Body Font

A bold, distinctive font for headlines paired with a simple, clean font for body text gives contrast without chaos — using more than two or three fonts in one design usually looks unplanned.

Match the Font's Feel to the Message

A playful, rounded font suits a birthday flyer; a clean, structured font suits a business report — the wrong pairing can undercut a message even if the words are right.

Readability Beats Personality for Body Text

Decorative or handwritten fonts might look interesting for a headline but become genuinely hard to read in long paragraphs — save personality fonts for short text only.

Reflection

  1. Think of a design you've seen with too many fonts. What effect did it have?
  2. Describe a message or event where a playful font would suit better than a formal one, or vice versa.
lessons.activity: Choose two fonts (one heading, one body) that suit a real design you're planning, and explain why the pairing fits the message.

lessons.title: Building a Color Palette That Feels Intentional
lessons.content:
Building a Color Palette That Feels Intentional

Color carries meaning and emotion — a well-chosen palette makes a design feel deliberate rather than random.

Limit Yourself to a Small Palette

Three to five colors (including a neutral like white or gray) is usually enough — more than that tends to compete for attention and looks unplanned.

Colors Carry Emotional Associations

Blue often reads as trustworthy or calm; red as urgent or energetic; green as growth or health — choosing colors that match your message's tone reinforces it, even subconsciously.

Canva's Color Palette Tools Help You Stay Consistent

Saving a brand kit or color palette in Canva means every new design pulls from the same set, instead of eyeballing colors freshly each time.

Reflection

  1. What emotional tone does the design you're planning need, and which colors support that?
  2. Have you seen a design with too many competing colors? What was the effect?
lessons.activity: Choose a 3-5 color palette for a real design project, explain the emotional tone each color supports, and save it as a reusable palette in Canva.

lessons.title: Keeping Designs On-Brand
lessons.content:
Keeping Designs On-Brand

Brand consistency is what lets someone recognize a design as yours (or your organization's) before they even read the text.

Consistency Builds Recognition Over Time

Using the same fonts, colors, and logo placement across every piece — social posts, flyers, presentations — builds recognition the way a company logo does, even without the actual logo present.

Canva's Brand Kit Locks In Your Choices

Setting up a Brand Kit with your fonts, colors, and logo means every new design starts from the same foundation, instead of recreating choices from memory each time.

Know When Consistency Should Flex

A seasonal or celebratory post might reasonably break from strict brand colors occasionally — the goal is recognizable consistency, not rigid sameness in every single piece.

Reflection

  1. Think of a brand (a business, a school, an organization) you recognize by its consistent visual style. What makes it recognizable?
  2. Would setting up a Brand Kit help a project you're working on? Why?
lessons.activity: Set up a simple Brand Kit in Canva with a font pairing, color palette, and logo (or placeholder), then create one design using it.

modules.title: Social Media Design

lessons.title: Sizing Content Correctly for Each Platform
lessons.content:
Sizing Content Correctly for Each Platform

A design built at the wrong size gets cropped, stretched, or awkwardly bordered when posted — sizing is the foundation everything else builds on.

Every Platform and Format Has Its Own Dimensions

A square Instagram post, a vertical Story, and a landscape Facebook cover all need different proportions — Canva's preset sizes for each platform remove the guesswork.

Designing at the Wrong Size Causes Real Problems

Text or faces near the edge of a square post can get cropped out when the platform displays it differently than expected — keeping key content safely away from edges prevents this.

Resizing Isn't Just Stretching

Canva's Resize tool can adapt a design to a new platform's dimensions, but elements often need repositioning afterward — a design rarely looks right by simply stretching the canvas.

Reflection

  1. Have you seen a social media post where text or an important element looked cropped off? What likely caused it?
  2. Why might simply stretching a square design to fit a vertical Story cause problems?
lessons.activity: Create a design at the correct preset size for one platform (like an Instagram post), then resize it for a different format (like a Story), adjusting the layout so nothing important is cropped.

materials.title: Platform Sizing Worksheet
materials.instructions: Create a design at the correct preset size for one platform (like an Instagram post), then resize it for a different format (like a Story), adjusting the layout so nothing important is cropped.

lessons.title: Designing Posts and Stories That Get Noticed
lessons.content:
Designing Posts and Stories That Get Noticed

A social media feed moves fast — a post has a fraction of a second to catch attention before someone scrolls past.

Lead With the Single Most Important Element

A cluttered post with five competing messages loses to a post with one clear headline or image — deciding the single most important thing to communicate first shapes everything else.

Stories Are Vertical and Momentary

Designed for full-screen vertical viewing and quick disappearance, Stories work best with bold, simple content readable in a couple of seconds — not dense paragraphs.

Leave Room for Platform Interface Elements

Profile icons, captions, and interactive stickers often overlay the top and bottom of a Story — keeping critical content in the safe middle zone avoids it being covered.

Reflection

  1. Think of a post that stopped your scrolling. What made it stand out in that split second?
  2. Why does a Story need simpler, bolder content than a regular feed post?
lessons.activity: Design one feed post and one Story for the same message, adapting the content density and layout appropriately for each format.

materials.title: Posts and Stories Worksheet
materials.instructions: Design one feed post and one Story for the same message, adapting the content density and layout appropriately for each format.

lessons.title: Building a Coherent Carousel
lessons.content:
Building a Coherent Carousel

A carousel (multiple swipeable slides in one post) lets you tell a fuller story, but only if the slides work together as a set.

Plan the Sequence Before Designing Each Slide

Deciding the order of ideas first (hook, then explanation, then call to action) keeps a carousel coherent — designing slides individually without a plan tends to produce a disconnected set.

Keep Visual Consistency Across Every Slide

The same fonts, colors, and layout structure across all slides makes a carousel feel like one connected piece, not several unrelated posts stitched together.

The First Slide Has to Earn the Swipe

If the opening slide doesn't hook attention, no one swipes to see the rest — it needs to work as a strong, complete post on its own.

Reflection

  1. Think of a carousel post you've swiped through fully. What made the first slide compelling?
  2. Why is visual consistency across slides important for a carousel specifically?
lessons.activity: Plan and design a 3-4 slide carousel with a clear sequence (hook, explanation, call to action) and consistent visual style across every slide.

options: Dense paragraphs of text

Identical to a regular feed post

modules.title: Flyers and Presentations

lessons.title: Designing a Flyer That Gets Read
lessons.content:
Designing a Flyer That Gets Read

A flyer has one job: communicate the essential information fast, to someone who probably won't read every word.

Lead With What, When, and Where

The event or offer name, date/time, and location should be the most visually prominent elements — everything else is secondary supporting detail.

One Clear Call to Action

A flyer should tell the reader exactly what to do next (register, call, visit) — burying the call to action in small text at the bottom is a common, avoidable mistake.

Don't Sacrifice Readability for Decoration

Busy backgrounds or excessive graphics behind text can make key information hard to read at a glance — the design should support the message, not compete with it.

Reflection

  1. Think of a flyer you've seen that clearly communicated what/when/where at a glance. What made it work?
  2. Describe a flyer that buried its call to action. Where should it have been instead?
lessons.activity: Design a flyer for a real or hypothetical event, making the what/when/where and a clear call to action the most visually prominent elements.

materials.title: Flyer Design Worksheet

lessons.title: Building a Presentation People Actually Follow
lessons.content:
Building a Presentation People Actually Follow

A presentation's job is to support a speaker, not replace them — slides packed with text work against both the speaker and the audience.

One Key Idea Per Slide

A slide with one headline and a supporting visual is far easier for an audience to absorb than a slide crammed with bullet points — if a slide needs a paragraph, it likely needs to be two slides.

Consistent Layout Keeps the Audience Oriented

Using the same title placement, font, and color scheme across every slide (via Canva's template) means the audience follows content, not new layouts, each time.

Visuals Should Clarify, Not Decorate

A chart, photo, or icon should help explain the point on that slide — a decorative image with no connection to the content just adds visual noise.

Reflection

  1. Think of a presentation you sat through that was hard to follow. What was on the slides?
  2. Why might a slide packed with bullet points actually work against a speaker instead of helping them?
lessons.activity: Build a 4-5 slide presentation on a real topic, with one key idea per slide, consistent layout throughout, and at least one visual that clarifies rather than decorates.

materials.title: Presentation Design Worksheet
materials.instructions: Build a 4-5 slide presentation on a real topic, with one key idea per slide, consistent layout throughout, and at least one visual that clarifies rather than decorates.

lessons.title: Simple Infographics That Explain at a Glance
lessons.content:
Simple Infographics That Explain at a Glance

An infographic turns information into something understood visually in seconds, rather than read line by line.

Start With the One Insight You Want Understood

Before choosing icons or colors, decide the single main takeaway — every element in the infographic should support that one insight, not compete with it.

Icons and Simple Charts Communicate Faster Than Paragraphs

A simple bar comparison or a row of icons representing a statistic communicates instantly, where a paragraph of numbers requires real reading effort.

Keep the Data Honest and Simple

An infographic should represent real numbers accurately — exaggerating a chart's proportions to make a point misleads the viewer, even unintentionally.

Reflection

  1. Think of an infographic you understood instantly. What made it clear at a glance?
  2. Why is it important that an infographic represents data honestly, not just persuasively?
lessons.activity: Create a simple one-page infographic communicating one real statistic or process, using icons or a simple chart rather than a paragraph of text.

materials.title: Infographics Worksheet

modules.title: Portfolio Project

lessons.title: Planning Your Coordinated Content Set
lessons.content:
Planning Your Coordinated Content Set

A strong portfolio piece isn't one great design — it's several designs that clearly belong together as a set.

Choose a Real Purpose to Design Around

A small brand identity for a club, business idea, or event (logo concept, social posts, a flyer) gives your set genuine purpose, rather than disconnected practice pieces.

Decide Your Brand Choices Before Designing Anything

Font pairing, color palette, and overall tone should be decided first — every piece in the set will pull from these same choices, which is what makes it look coordinated.

List the Specific Pieces Your Set Will Include

Deciding upfront exactly what you're building (e.g., one flyer, two social posts, one presentation cover) keeps the project focused and achievable.

Reflection

  1. What real purpose (club, business idea, event, cause) will you design your coordinated set around?
  2. What specific pieces will your set include, and what brand choices will tie them together?

lessons.title: Building the Full Set
lessons.content:
Building the Full Set

This is where every skill from earlier modules — alignment, hierarchy, typography, color, sizing — comes together into one coordinated body of work.

Build One Piece First as Your Reference

Designing your first piece carefully, then using it as the visual reference for the rest, keeps the whole set consistent without constantly re-deciding choices.

Reuse Elements Deliberately Across Pieces

Reusing the same logo placement, color blocks, or icon style across different pieces (a flyer, a post, a presentation cover) is what makes a set read as one coordinated project, not separate designs.

Check Consistency As You Go, Not Just at the End

Comparing each new piece against your first one as you build catches drift in color or font choice early, before it's repeated across the whole set.

Reflection

  1. Which piece from your plan will you build first, and why does it make a good reference?
  2. What specific elements (logo, color block, icon style) will you reuse across your set?
lessons.activity: Build your full coordinated content set (all pieces from your plan), reusing consistent elements across each piece.

lessons.title: Reviewing and Presenting Your Portfolio Set
lessons.content:
Reviewing and Presenting Your Portfolio Set

A finished set isn't done until it's been checked for consistency and you can explain the choices behind it.

Compare Every Piece Side by Side

Viewing all your pieces together (not one at a time) makes any inconsistency in color, font, or spacing immediately obvious — a check that's hard to do while designing one piece at a time.

Export Each Piece in the Right Format

A social post exports differently than a flyer meant for print — checking the correct format and size for each piece's actual use avoids a set that looks great in Canva but fails when used.

Explain Your Design Decisions

Being able to explain why you chose this palette, this hierarchy, this layout turns your set into demonstrated skill — not just a collection of pretty images.

Reflection

  1. Compare your pieces side by side. Is there any inconsistency you can now spot?
  2. What are two specific design decisions you can clearly explain the reasoning behind?

Recognize common phishing and scam patterns.
Protect devices and personal information.
Use public and shared technology more safely.
Respond appropriately to suspected compromise.
