modules.title: Cybersecurity Basics
modules.description: Threats, risk, personal responsibility and common attack methods.

lessons.title: Why You're a Target, Even With Nothing to Hide
lessons.content:
Why You're a Target, Even With Nothing to Hide

"I have nothing worth stealing" is one of the most common and most mistaken assumptions in cybersecurity.

Attackers Want Access, Not Just Money

A compromised email or social account can be used to scam your contacts, spread malware, or access other accounts through password resets — you don't need to be wealthy or important to be useful to an attacker.

Most Attacks Are Automated, Not Personal

The majority of attacks aren't a hacker specifically targeting you — they're automated systems testing thousands of accounts for weak passwords or unpatched software, and anyone can be caught in that net.

Security Is Everyone's Responsibility, Not Just IT's

Most successful attacks exploit a human decision (clicking a link, reusing a password) rather than a purely technical flaw — meaning your daily habits are a real part of the defense, not someone else's job.

Reflection

  1. Before this lesson, did you assume you weren't a realistic target? What changed your thinking?
  2. Describe a way a compromised personal account could be used to harm people you know.
lessons.activity: List three accounts you use regularly and describe what an attacker could realistically do if each one were compromised, even if you don't consider yourself a high-value target.

materials.title: Understanding Your Risk Worksheet
materials.instructions: List three accounts you use regularly and describe what an attacker could realistically do if each one were compromised, even if you don't consider yourself a high-value target.

lessons.title: The Most Common Attack Methods
lessons.content:
The Most Common Attack Methods

Most cyberattacks fall into a handful of familiar categories — recognizing the pattern matters more than memorizing technical jargon.

Phishing: Tricking You Into Acting

A fake message designed to look legitimate, aiming to get you to click a bad link, download malware, or hand over credentials — covered in depth later in this course.

Malware: Software Designed to Cause Harm

Malicious software that can steal data, lock your files for ransom, or spy on your activity — often installed through a deceptive download or a compromised link.

Credential Stuffing: Reusing Stolen Passwords

Attackers take passwords leaked from one breached site and try them on other sites automatically — this is exactly why password reuse is so dangerous, even for "unimportant" accounts.

Reflection

  1. Which of these three attack types have you encountered or heard about happening to someone you know?
  2. Why does credential stuffing make reusing passwords across sites especially risky?
lessons.activity: Research (or recall) a real example of one of these attack types affecting a person, school, or organization, and describe what actually happened.

materials.title: Attack Methods Worksheet
materials.instructions: Research (or recall) a real example of one of these attack types affecting a person, school, or organization, and describe what actually happened.

lessons.title: Thinking in Terms of Risk, Not Fear
lessons.content:
Thinking in Terms of Risk, Not Fear

Good cybersecurity habits come from realistic risk assessment, not from either paranoia or complacency.

Ask What's Actually at Stake

Weighing what an account or device actually holds (personal photos, financial access, school records) helps you decide how much protection it genuinely needs — not every account needs the same level of caution.

Small, Consistent Habits Beat Occasional Vigilance

Reliable habits — updating software, unique passwords, pausing before clicking — protect you far more consistently than only being careful when you happen to feel suspicious.

Perfect Security Doesn't Exist, Reasonable Precaution Does

No individual can eliminate all risk — the realistic goal is making yourself a harder, less convenient target than the next person, which is often enough to avoid most automated attacks.

Reflection

  1. Which of your accounts genuinely holds the most sensitive information, and are your habits around it matched to that?
  2. Describe one small habit you could build consistently, rather than relying on occasional vigilance.
lessons.activity: List your most sensitive accounts or devices, rank them by what's actually at stake, and identify one consistent habit you'll build to protect the highest-risk one.

materials.title: Risk Assessment Worksheet
materials.instructions: List your most sensitive accounts or devices, rank them by what's actually at stake, and identify one consistent habit you'll build to protect the highest-risk one.

questions.question: This module explains that a compromised personal account is valuable to attackers because it can:
options: Only be used if the owner is wealthy
Be used to scam contacts or access other accounts
Never actually be misused
Only affect large organizations
questions.explanation: Even an ordinary personal account can be used to scam contacts or gain access to other linked accounts.

questions.question: According to this module, credential stuffing works by:
options: Guessing passwords completely at random
Trying passwords leaked from one breach on other sites
Only targeting one specific person at a time
Requiring physical access to a device
questions.explanation: Credential stuffing reuses passwords leaked from one breached site to try logging into other sites automatically.

questions.question: This module recommends approaching personal cybersecurity by:
options: Assuming perfect security is achievable
Building consistent habits based on realistic risk, not fear
Only worrying about security when something feels suspicious
Ignoring risk assessment entirely
questions.explanation: Realistic risk assessment and consistent habits are more effective than occasional vigilance or assuming perfect safety.

modules.title: Passwords and Authentication
modules.description: Strong passwords, password managers and MFA.

lessons.title: What Makes a Password Actually Strong
lessons.content:
What Makes a Password Actually Strong

Length matters more than complexity — a long passphrase is often stronger and easier to remember than a short jumble of symbols.

Length Beats Cleverness

A password like "correct-horse-battery-staple" (four random words) is dramatically harder for a computer to crack than "P@ss1!" despite looking simpler — attackers guess length and pattern combinations, and every extra character multiplies the guessing time enormously.

Why Reuse Is the Real Danger

The strongest password in the world becomes worthless the moment it's reused, because one breached site can expose it for every other account using the same one — uniqueness matters as much as strength.

Predictable Patterns Are Not Secret

Substituting "a" with "@" or adding "123" to the end of a familiar word is a pattern attackers' cracking tools already account for — it barely slows them down, even though it feels clever.

Reflection

  1. Look at your current passwords honestly — are any of them reused across multiple accounts?
  2. Try building one four-word passphrase right now. How does it compare in memorability to a complex short password?
lessons.activity: Audit five of your real accounts (without writing down actual passwords) and note which ones share a password or use a predictable pattern. Rewrite one as a strong, unique passphrase.

materials.title: Password Strength Audit
materials.instructions: Audit five of your real accounts (without writing down actual passwords) and note which ones share a password or use a predictable pattern. Rewrite one as a strong, unique passphrase.

lessons.title: Password Managers: Why You Need One
lessons.content:
Password Managers: Why You Need One

No one can memorize dozens of unique, strong passwords — a password manager is what makes uniqueness actually realistic.

What a Password Manager Actually Does

It generates and stores a strong, unique password for every account behind one master password (or biometric unlock), auto-filling credentials so you never have to remember or retype them.

Why This Beats Reuse or a Notebook

Reused passwords collapse under a single breach, and paper notes get lost or seen — an encrypted manager keeps every credential unique and accessible only to you, syncing safely across your devices.

The One Password You Do Need to Remember

Your master password becomes the single point of protection for everything else, so it deserves to be your longest, most unique passphrase — and should always be paired with multi-factor authentication where the manager supports it.

Reflection

  1. What has stopped you from using a password manager so far — convenience, trust, or simply not knowing where to start?
  2. What would you look for before trusting a password manager with your accounts?
lessons.activity: Research two reputable password managers (built into your browser/phone counts) and compare one feature each offers. Decide which fits your situation and explain why.

materials.title: Password Manager Comparison
materials.instructions: Research two reputable password managers (built into your browser/phone counts) and compare one feature each offers. Decide which fits your situation and explain why.

lessons.title: Multi-Factor Authentication: Your Second Lock
lessons.content:
Multi-Factor Authentication: Your Second Lock

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) means proving who you are with something beyond just a password — and it's the single most effective step most people can take to protect an account.

Why a Password Alone Isn't Enough

Passwords can be leaked, guessed, or phished without you ever knowing — MFA means a stolen password alone isn't enough to get in, because the attacker still needs your second factor.

The Common Forms MFA Takes

An authenticator app code, a text message code, a physical security key, or a biometric scan are the most common second factors — authenticator apps and security keys are generally considered stronger than text messages, which can be intercepted through SIM-swap scams.

Turn It On Everywhere It Matters Most

Email, banking, and any account tied to password resets for other accounts deserve MFA first — because a compromised email is often the master key an attacker uses to break into everything else.

Reflection

  1. Which of your accounts already has MFA enabled, and which important one is still missing it?
  2. Why is your email account often the highest-priority place to enable MFA?
lessons.activity: Enable MFA on one account that doesn't already have it (starting with email is recommended), and describe which method you chose and why.

materials.title: MFA Setup Log
materials.instructions: Enable MFA on one account that doesn't already have it (starting with email is recommended), and describe which method you chose and why.

questions.question: According to this module, what makes a password genuinely strong?
options: Substituting letters with symbols, like @ for a
Length and uniqueness, such as a long passphrase
Using the same strong password everywhere for consistency
Adding your birth year to the end
questions.explanation: Length and uniqueness (such as a random four-word passphrase) matter far more than symbol substitution or complexity alone.

questions.question: This module explains that a password manager is valuable mainly because it:
options: Eliminates the need for any master password
Makes using a unique, strong password for every account realistic
Is only useful for businesses, not individuals
Replaces the need for multi-factor authentication
questions.explanation: A password manager generates and stores unique strong passwords for every account, making uniqueness practical without requiring memorization.

questions.question: Why does this module recommend enabling MFA on your email account first?
options: Email is rarely targeted by attackers
Email is often used to reset passwords for other accounts, making it a master key
MFA on email is required by law
Email accounts don't support strong passwords
questions.explanation: Because email is commonly used to reset passwords for other accounts, a compromised email can cascade into many other compromised accounts.

modules.title: Phishing and Social Engineering
modules.description: Suspicious messages, links, urgency and verification.

lessons.title: Recognizing a Phishing Attempt
lessons.content:
Recognizing a Phishing Attempt

Phishing is a message designed to trick you into clicking a bad link, downloading malware, or handing over information — and the best ones are convincing on purpose.

The Sender Doesn't Have to Be Real

A display name can say anything — always check the actual email address or number, not just the name shown, since "IT Support" is trivial to fake as a display name.

Links Rarely Go Where They Claim

Hovering over a link (without clicking) reveals its real destination — a mismatch between the visible text and the actual URL, or a domain that's almost-but-not-quite right (like "paypa1.com"), is a strong warning sign.

Urgency Is the Most Common Trick

"Your account will be suspended in 24 hours" or "urgent action required" is designed to make you act before you think — legitimate organizations rarely demand instant action through a single unsolicited message.

Reflection

  1. Think of a suspicious message you've received. What made it feel "off" even before you analyzed it closely?
  2. Why does urgency work so well as a manipulation tactic?
lessons.activity: Find (or recall) one real phishing message you've received. Identify at least three specific red flags in it: sender, links, urgency language, or requests.

materials.title: Phishing Red Flags Worksheet
materials.instructions: Find (or recall) one real phishing message you've received. Identify at least three specific red flags in it: sender, links, urgency language, or requests.

lessons.title: Social Engineering Beyond Email
lessons.content:
Social Engineering Beyond Email

Social engineering is manipulating people (not systems) into giving up access or information — and it happens over text, phone calls, and social media just as often as email.

Vishing: Voice Phishing Over the Phone

A caller pretending to be from your bank, a government agency, or tech support, creating pressure to act — real institutions rarely call demanding immediate payment or your password over the phone.

Smishing: Phishing by Text Message

A text claiming a package delivery issue or a prize you've won, with a link designed to steal information — the same red flags (urgency, mismatched links, unexpected requests) apply here too.

Pretexting: Building a Believable Story

An attacker researching you or your workplace to build a convincing scenario ("I'm calling on behalf of your manager about...") — the more personalized an unsolicited request feels, the more it deserves independent verification, not less.

Reflection

  1. Have you or someone you know received a suspicious phone call or text? What was the tactic being used?
  2. Why might a highly personalized message actually be more dangerous than a generic one?
lessons.activity: Describe one realistic vishing or smishing scenario targeting someone in your life, and write the exact verification step they should take before responding.

materials.title: Social Engineering Scenario Worksheet
materials.instructions: Describe one realistic vishing or smishing scenario targeting someone in your life, and write the exact verification step they should take before responding.

lessons.title: Verify Before You Trust
lessons.content:
Verify Before You Trust

The single most reliable defense against phishing and social engineering is a simple habit: verify through a separate, known channel before acting.

Never Verify Using the Contact Info Provided

If a suspicious email gives you a phone number to call, don't use it — the number can be fake too. Instead, look up the organization's number independently or use a saved contact.

Slow Down When You Feel Pressured

The moment you notice urgency, fear, or excitement pushing you to act fast, treat that feeling itself as the warning sign — pausing for even a minute is often enough to spot the trick.

Reporting Helps Everyone, Not Just You

Reporting a phishing attempt (to your email provider, employer, or platform) can get the message blocked before it reaches others — staying quiet about a near-miss helps no one.

Reflection

  1. Describe a "verify through a separate channel" step you could realistically take the next time something feels off.
  2. Why is reporting a suspicious message valuable even if you didn't fall for it?
lessons.activity: Write a personal three-step checklist you'll follow the next time you receive a message that creates urgency or asks for sensitive information.

materials.title: Verify-Before-Trust Checklist
materials.instructions: Write a personal three-step checklist you'll follow the next time you receive a message that creates urgency or asks for sensitive information.

questions.question: According to this module, why is a display name alone not enough to trust a sender?
options: Display names cannot be changed by attackers
Display names are trivial to fake, so the actual address must be checked
Display names are only used in phone calls
Email providers block all fake display names automatically
questions.explanation: A display name can say anything; the actual email address or phone number must be checked to verify the real sender.

questions.question: This module describes 'smishing' as:
options: Phishing conducted through text messages
A type of strong password
A form of multi-factor authentication
A legitimate customer service tool
questions.explanation: Smishing is phishing carried out through text messages, often using urgency and suspicious links, just like email phishing.

questions.question: What does this module recommend as the most reliable defense against phishing and social engineering?
options: Responding quickly to resolve the issue before it escalates
Using the contact information provided in the suspicious message
Verifying through a separate, independently known channel before acting
Ignoring all unexpected messages permanently
questions.explanation: Verifying independently, rather than through contact details given in the suspicious message itself, is the most reliable defense.

modules.title: Device and Network Safety
modules.description: Updates, malware, Wi-Fi and backups.

lessons.title: Updates and Malware: Keeping Devices Clean
lessons.content:
Updates and Malware: Keeping Devices Clean

Software updates aren't just new features — most exist to patch security vulnerabilities that attackers actively exploit.

Why "I'll Update Later" Is Risky

Once a vulnerability is publicly patched, attackers know exactly what unpatched devices are missing — delaying updates leaves a known, documented door open.

Malware Doesn't Always Look Suspicious

Malicious software can hide inside a cracked app, a fake browser extension, or an infected USB drive — it can run quietly in the background stealing data long before you notice anything wrong.

Install Only From Trusted Sources

Official app stores and verified publisher websites screen for malware far more reliably than random download links — a "free" version of paid software from an unofficial site is one of the most common malware delivery methods.

Reflection

  1. Do you currently have automatic updates enabled on your main devices? If not, why not?
  2. Describe one habit around downloading apps or files that you should reconsider.
lessons.activity: Check your phone and computer for pending updates right now. Install them, and note how many days or versions behind each device was.

materials.title: Device Update Check
materials.instructions: Check your phone and computer for pending updates right now. Install them, and note how many days or versions behind each device was.

lessons.title: Staying Safe on Wi-Fi Networks
lessons.content:
Staying Safe on Wi-Fi Networks

Public Wi-Fi is convenient, but an open network is a shared space — anything unencrypted traveling across it can potentially be seen by others on the same network.

What Makes Public Wi-Fi Risky

An open network with no password (common in cafes and airports) offers no encryption between your device and the router — a nearby attacker on the same network can potentially intercept unencrypted traffic.

Practical Habits That Reduce the Risk

Avoid logging into sensitive accounts (banking, email) on public Wi-Fi when possible, look for "https" in website addresses (which encrypts the connection to that specific site), and consider a reputable VPN for an added layer of protection on untrusted networks.

Your Home Network Deserves Attention Too

A default router password, an outdated router, or a network name broadcasting your address are all avoidable risks — changing default credentials and keeping router firmware updated protects everyone using that network.

Reflection

  1. Think of a recent time you used public Wi-Fi. What, if anything, did you do to protect your connection?
  2. Have you ever changed your home router's default password? Why does that matter?
lessons.activity: Check your home router's settings (or ask whoever manages it) to confirm the default admin password has been changed. Document what you found.

materials.title: Wi-Fi Safety Check
materials.instructions: Check your home router's settings (or ask whoever manages it) to confirm the default admin password has been changed. Document what you found.

lessons.title: Backups: Your Safety Net
lessons.content:
Backups: Your Safety Net

A backup is a copy of your important data stored somewhere separate from your main device — and it's the single best protection against ransomware, device loss, or hardware failure.

Why Backups Matter Even If You're Careful

Even the most cautious person can lose a device, suffer a hardware failure, or fall victim to a well-crafted attack — a backup means that worst-case scenario costs you inconvenience, not everything.

The 3-2-1 Habit, Simplified

Keep important data in at least two places, with one of them not permanently connected to your main device — a cloud backup plus an occasional external drive backup covers most personal needs without requiring anything complicated.

Backups Only Help If They're Recent and Tested

A backup from two years ago is much less useful than one from last week — set a reminder to check that backups are actually running, and occasionally confirm you can actually restore a file from one.

Reflection

  1. Do you currently back up your most important files? If something happened to your device today, what would you lose?
  2. What's one realistic backup habit you could start this week?
lessons.activity: Identify your three most important files or folders. Back them up today using a cloud service or external drive, and describe the method you used.

materials.title: Personal Backup Plan
materials.instructions: Identify your three most important files or folders. Back them up today using a cloud service or external drive, and describe the method you used.

questions.question: According to this module, why is delaying software updates risky?
options: Updates always slow devices down permanently
Once a vulnerability is publicly patched, attackers know what unpatched devices are missing
Updates are optional and rarely relate to security
Only business devices need regular updates
questions.explanation: Once a patch is released, the vulnerability it fixes becomes public knowledge, making unpatched devices an easy known target.

questions.question: This module explains that the main risk of open public Wi-Fi is:
options: It costs more than home internet
Unencrypted traffic can potentially be intercepted by others on the same network
It only works for browsing, not logging in
It automatically installs malware on connection
questions.explanation: Open networks with no password offer no encryption, meaning unencrypted traffic could potentially be seen by others sharing the network.

questions.question: According to this module, a backup is most valuable when it is:
options: Stored only on the same device it protects
Made once and never checked again
Recent and periodically tested to confirm it can be restored
Kept exclusively on paper
questions.explanation: A backup is only useful if it is reasonably recent and has actually been confirmed to restore correctly when needed.

modules.title: Privacy and Digital Footprint
modules.description: Permissions, oversharing, scams and data protection.

lessons.title: Understanding App Permissions
lessons.content:
Understanding App Permissions

Every time an app asks for access to your location, contacts, camera, or microphone, that's a real decision worth pausing on — not a formality to click through.

Ask Whether the Permission Makes Sense

A flashlight app requesting access to your contacts and location has no functional reason to need either — when a permission request doesn't match what the app actually does, that's worth questioning.

Permissions Can Usually Be Reviewed and Revoked

Most phones let you review and turn off individual app permissions after installation — periodically checking which apps have access to your camera, microphone, or location is a healthy habit, not paranoia.

Default Settings Favor Data Collection

Many apps default to the most permissive settings possible because broader access benefits the app, not necessarily you — adjusting privacy settings after installing something new takes a few minutes and is usually worth it.

Reflection

  1. Pick one app on your phone and check what permissions it currently has. Did anything surprise you?
  2. Why might an app default to more permissive settings than most users actually need?
lessons.activity: Review the permissions on three apps on your phone. Revoke at least one permission that doesn't match what the app actually needs to function.

materials.title: App Permissions Audit
materials.instructions: Review the permissions on three apps on your phone. Revoke at least one permission that doesn't match what the app actually needs to function.

lessons.title: Your Digital Footprint and Oversharing
lessons.content:
Your Digital Footprint and Oversharing

Your digital footprint is the trail of information you leave behind through posts, profiles, comments, and data attached to your accounts — and it's often more visible and permanent than it feels in the moment.

Small Details Add Up

A vacation post revealing you're away from home, a school or workplace tagged in your bio, a birthdate in a public profile — individually minor, but combined they can build a surprisingly complete picture for someone with bad intentions.

Once Posted, Assume It's Permanent

Screenshots, archives, and shares mean deleting a post doesn't guarantee it's gone — think about whether you'd be comfortable with a stranger, employer, or scammer seeing it before you post, not after.

Review Your Privacy Settings Periodically

Social media platforms change their privacy settings and defaults over time — a setting you configured carefully two years ago may not reflect the platform's current options or your current audience.

Reflection

  1. Search your own name (or think about what's publicly visible on your main social profile). Is there anything there you'd want to reconsider?
  2. Describe one habit that could reduce how much personal information you share without meaning to.
lessons.activity: Review the privacy settings on your most-used social media account. List two changes you made or considered making, and why.

materials.title: Digital Footprint Privacy Review
materials.instructions: Review the privacy settings on your most-used social media account. List two changes you made or considered making, and why.

lessons.title: Recognizing Scams That Target Trust
lessons.content:
Recognizing Scams That Target Trust

Many scams don't rely on technical tricks at all — they rely on exploiting trust, generosity, or hope.

"Too Good to Be True" Usually Is

Unexpected prize winnings, investment opportunities promising guaranteed returns, or a stranger offering a large sum of money for a small upfront fee — these follow a recognizable pattern regardless of the specific story used.

Romance and Relationship Scams Are Real and Common

An online relationship that moves quickly toward emotional intimacy and eventually toward requests for money is a well-documented scam pattern — genuine relationships don't typically require secrecy or urgent financial help from someone you've never met in person.

Protect People Around You Too

Older relatives and people newer to the internet are disproportionately targeted by scams — sharing what you learn in this lesson with them is a genuinely useful way to extend its impact.

Reflection

  1. Have you or someone you know encountered a scam that used one of these patterns? What made it convincing at first?
  2. Who in your life might benefit from a conversation about these scam patterns?
lessons.activity: Have a short conversation with a family member or friend about one scam pattern from this lesson. Write down what they already knew and what was new to them.

materials.title: Scam Awareness Conversation Log
materials.instructions: Have a short conversation with a family member or friend about one scam pattern from this lesson. Write down what they already knew and what was new to them.

questions.question: According to this module, when should an app permission request raise concern?
options: Whenever an app requests any permission at all
When the permission doesn't match what the app actually needs to function
Only when the app is free to download
Permissions never need to be questioned
questions.explanation: A permission request that doesn't match the app's actual function (like a flashlight app requesting contacts) is a reasonable reason to question or deny it.

questions.question: This module explains that once something is posted online, you should generally assume:
options: It disappears completely once deleted
It may be permanent due to screenshots, archives, or shares
Only the platform can ever see it
It cannot affect your digital footprint
questions.explanation: Screenshots, archives, and shares mean that deleting a post does not guarantee the information is truly gone.

questions.question: What common pattern does this module identify across many scams, including romance scams?
options: They always involve a phone call from a blocked number
They exploit trust, urgency, or emotional connection rather than technical tricks
They only target businesses, never individuals
They require advanced technical skill to fall for
questions.explanation: Many scams succeed by exploiting trust, generosity, urgency, or emotional connection rather than relying on technical sophistication.

modules.title: Incident Response
modules.description: What to do after a suspicious click, account compromise or lost device.

lessons.title: You Clicked Something Suspicious. Now What?
lessons.content:
You Clicked Something Suspicious. Now What?

Realizing you clicked a bad link or opened a suspicious attachment is uncomfortable — but what you do in the next few minutes matters far more than the mistake itself.

Disconnect First, Investigate Second

If you suspect malware, disconnecting the device from Wi-Fi (or turning on airplane mode) can limit an attacker's ability to communicate with or control the device further while you figure out what happened.

Change Passwords From a Different, Trusted Device

If the click involved entering credentials on a fake site, change that password immediately from a separate, trusted device — and change it on any other account sharing the same password.

Run a Security Scan and Watch for Odd Behavior

A reputable antivirus/security scan can catch known malware — and afterward, stay alert for unusual pop-ups, unexpected account activity, or unfamiliar new apps as signs something may still be wrong.

Reflection

  1. Before this lesson, would you have known these first steps? What would you have done instead?
  2. Why does disconnecting from the network come before other investigation steps?
lessons.activity: Write a personal step-by-step response plan for 'I think I clicked something suspicious' that you could follow calmly under stress.

materials.title: Suspicious Click Response Plan
materials.instructions: Write a personal step-by-step response plan for 'I think I clicked something suspicious' that you could follow calmly under stress.

lessons.title: Responding to a Compromised Account
lessons.content:
Responding to a Compromised Account

Signs of a compromised account — password no longer working, unfamiliar sent messages, unrecognized login alerts — call for fast, specific action.

Regain Access Through Official Recovery

Use the platform's official "forgot password" or account recovery process immediately — acting quickly improves your chances before an attacker changes recovery information and locks you out completely.

Check and Revoke Unfamiliar Access

Once back in, review connected apps, active sessions, and forwarding rules (a common trick in compromised email accounts is a hidden forwarding rule silently copying your messages elsewhere) and remove anything unfamiliar.

Warn Your Contacts

A compromised account is often used to scam the people who trust you — a quick, honest message to close contacts warning them to ignore recent messages can prevent them from becoming victims too.

Reflection

  1. What's the fastest way you could verify whether one of your accounts has been compromised right now?
  2. Why is checking for a hidden forwarding rule an important step after recovering a compromised email account?
lessons.activity: Check the active sessions or connected apps list on one of your important accounts right now. Document what you found and remove anything unfamiliar.

materials.title: Account Compromise Response Checklist
materials.instructions: Check the active sessions or connected apps list on one of your important accounts right now. Document what you found and remove anything unfamiliar.

lessons.title: Losing a Device: Acting Fast
lessons.content:
Losing a Device: Acting Fast

A lost or stolen device is stressful, but the accounts and data it holds are what's actually at risk — and most of that risk can be contained quickly if you act right away.

Use Remote Lock and Wipe Tools

Most phones and laptops have a built-in "find my device" feature that can remotely lock, locate, or wipe the device — knowing this feature is enabled and how to access it before you ever need it saves critical time.

Log Out of Accounts Remotely Where Possible

Many services let you remotely sign out active sessions on a specific device from a browser on another device — this cuts off access even if the device itself can't be recovered.

Report It, Especially for Work or School Devices

Reporting a lost device to your school, employer, or carrier promptly can trigger additional protections and is often required — delaying the report out of embarrassment only increases the risk window.

Reflection

  1. Do you know how to remotely lock or wipe your primary device? If not, what would stop you from setting that up today?
  2. Why might reporting a lost device quickly matter even if you're embarrassed about losing it?
lessons.activity: Confirm that 'find my device' (or equivalent) is enabled on your primary phone or laptop. If it isn't, turn it on and document the steps you took.

materials.title: Device Loss Preparedness Check
materials.instructions: Confirm that 'find my device' (or equivalent) is enabled on your primary phone or laptop. If it isn't, turn it on and document the steps you took.

questions.question: According to this module, why should you disconnect a device from the network if you suspect malware?
options: To limit an attacker's ability to communicate with or control the device further
It permanently deletes any malware present
It is required before any password can be changed
It has no real security benefit
questions.explanation: Disconnecting from the network can limit an attacker's ability to communicate with or further control a compromised device.

questions.question: This module identifies which of the following as a common hidden trick after email compromise?
options: A forwarding rule silently copying your messages elsewhere
An automatic permanent account deletion
A mandatory password reset every day
A visible pop-up warning on every login
questions.explanation: Attackers sometimes set up a hidden forwarding rule to silently copy a compromised account's messages, which is why checking for one is an important recovery step.

questions.question: Why does this module recommend confirming 'find my device' is enabled before you ever need it?
options: It cannot be enabled after a device is lost
Knowing it's ready in advance saves critical time if a device is lost or stolen
It is only useful for company-owned devices
It automatically prevents all device theft
questions.explanation: Being familiar with remote lock/wipe tools in advance means you can act quickly and effectively if a device is actually lost or stolen.

questions.question: Why is an ordinary personal account still a valuable target for attackers?
options: It can be used to scam contacts or access linked accounts
Attackers only target wealthy individuals
Personal accounts cannot be compromised
It has no value unless it holds financial data
questions.explanation: Even accounts with no direct financial value can be used to scam contacts or gain access to other linked accounts.

questions.question: What makes a passphrase like a string of four random words stronger than a short, complex password?
options: It uses more special characters
Its greater length makes it much harder to crack, despite being easier to remember
It is shorter and simpler to guess
It never needs to be changed
questions.explanation: Length matters more than complexity; a long passphrase is dramatically harder to crack than a short, complex password.

questions.question: Why does this course recommend enabling multi-factor authentication on your email account first?
options: Email is rarely a target for attackers
Email is often used to reset passwords for other accounts, making it a master key
MFA is only available for email accounts
Email accounts cannot use strong passwords
questions.explanation: Because email often controls password resets for other accounts, protecting it with MFA has an outsized impact on your overall security.

questions.question: What is the most reliable way to verify a suspicious message asking for sensitive information or urgent action?
options: Reply directly to the message asking if it's real
Call the number provided in the suspicious message
Verify independently through a separately known, trusted contact method
Comply quickly to avoid any consequences
questions.explanation: Verifying through an independently known channel, not the contact details in the suspicious message itself, is the most reliable defense.

questions.question: Why should devices and applications be kept updated?
options: Updates are optional and mostly cosmetic
Updates patch known security vulnerabilities that attackers actively exploit
Updates only affect device speed, not security
Only workplace devices need to be updated
questions.explanation: Security updates patch known vulnerabilities; delaying them leaves a documented, exploitable gap open.

questions.question: Why should app permissions be reviewed rather than accepted automatically?
options: Apps never request unnecessary permissions
A permission that doesn't match what the app actually does is worth questioning
Reviewing permissions is required by every app store
Permissions cannot be changed after installation
questions.explanation: When a requested permission doesn't align with what an app actually needs to function, it deserves scrutiny rather than automatic approval.

questions.question: What should you assume about anything you post online, even if later deleted?
options: It disappears completely and permanently once deleted
It may still exist through screenshots, archives, or shares
Only you can ever see what you post
Deletion guarantees full removal everywhere
questions.explanation: Screenshots, archives, and shares mean that deleting a post does not guarantee the information is truly gone.

questions.question: What is the recommended first step if you suspect your device has malware after clicking a suspicious link?
options: Immediately share the incident publicly online
Disconnect the device from the network to limit further damage
Ignore it and wait to see if problems appear
Install as many new apps as possible
questions.explanation: Disconnecting the device from the network can limit an attacker's ability to communicate with or further control it while you investigate.
